title: NAS weighs in more than 33kg heavier than Paul Gallen
text:
Nelson Asofa-Solomona has landed another low blow on Paul Gallen, claiming that even his premiership-winning former Cronulla teammates want the Sharks legend laid out on Friday night.

A day after the Big Nasty riled his rival by dragging Gallen's wife into the verbal sledging, Asofa-Solomona got even nastier as he lobbed explosive accusations about the Sharks' only grand final-winning captain.

"There's been so many people jumping in my DMs," Asofa-Solomona said on Thursday.

"People that have played with him, people that have played against him, people who have worked with them in the past. They were telling me all these stories about him and saying 'Yeah, bro, please do a job on him.'

"That was my plan all along anyway."

Nelson Asofa-Solomona says his plan is to knock Paul Gallen out. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

The Cronulla-Melbourne rivalry is one of the fiercest in the NRL, with the two sides featuring in a series of spiteful encounters either side the Sharks' stirring 2016 grand final triumph over the Storm.

Having already copped a drugs spray from Asofa-Solomona (3-0, 3KOs) in light of the Cronulla peptides saga, Gallen (16-2-1, 8KOs) will be livid after the ex-Storm star's latest verbal jabs.

Asofa-Solomona would not be drawn on specifics but said Gallen's former State of Origin teammates and "work colleagues" were among those who he claimed had reached out to him in the hope of doing over the 2014 series-winning Blues skipper.

"I can't say too much, but probably just stuff to do with money and bits and pieces," Asofa-Solomona said.

"But, look, he's grown up in a different era. He's a bit of a different cat, but the new era is here."

Asofa-Solomona's inflammatory allegations came after the two heavyweights featured in a spicy weigh-in at Sydney's TikTok Entertainment Centre.

The ex-New Zealand Test enforcer promised Gallen he would proudly take the mantle of NRL-boxing crossover king on Friday night.

"And if it's not a knockout, I don't want it," the 200cm, 137.56-kilogram behemoth said.

"That's the only result I'm here to get. I'm here for a highlight-reel finish."

Nelson Asofa-Solomona is much heavier than Paul Gallen. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

But the retiring Gallen, 45, is having none of it, despite weighing in at 104.18kg.

"I'm really proud I'm fighting a bloke now, 30-odd kilos heavier than me, 15 years younger than me and I'm still willing to compete — and I'll win this fight, at my age," he said.

"That's what I'm proud of, and this is a no-lose situation for me. I'm going to get paid a ton of money and go home happy and healthy and live the rest of my life with my family.

"That's my goal in life and that's what I'm here to do."

What time is the fight?

Paul Gallen and Nelson Asofa-Solomona meet on Friday, November 6, with the main card getting underway from 7:00pm AEDT.

How can I watch the fight?

The fight is exclusive to Fox Sports and Kayo's pay per view channel, Main Event and will cost $69.95.

ABC Sport will live-blog the fight card.

Who else is fighting?

Here's the card.

title: IVF, abortion and more set to cease at Newcastle private hospitals
text:
Calvary Health Care will cease IVF, elective abortions, voluntary assisted dying, and gender reassignment procedures if it acquires two Newcastle-based private hospitals later this month.

The Catholic provider is planning to take over 14 hospitals across the country, including Newcastle and Hunter Valley Private hospitals, after Healthscope collapsed earlier this year.

The hospital sales are still subject to regulatory approvals, including the transfer of a state government-issued hospital licence and a determination from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC).

Calvary follows a Catholic code of ethics, which prohibits providers from offering a range of reproductive and community health services on religious grounds.

For the past week, concerns have been spreading about what the changes mean for women's and community health.

Rachel Hughes says religion should not interfere with healthcare. (Supplied: Rachel Hughes)

Vice-president of the Hunter Workers Women's Committee Rachel Hughes said religion should have no place in health care.

"What happens to people's bodies should be a choice between them and their medical practitioner," she said.

"It should have nothing to do with the operator of the hospital; it should have nothing to do with religion."

Ms Hughes said she was most worried about the impact the changes would have on women and those trying for a family.

"[The hospital] is one of very few places outside of Sydney within New South Wales offering IVF procedures," she said.

" There's a broader impact on families, on marriages, on children … this is not fair. "

Peter Harrigan has worked at Newcastle Private Hospital for 20 years. (ABC Newcastle: Ben Clifford)

Peter Harrigan has worked as an anaesthetist at Newcastle Private Hospital for 20 years.

Dr Harrigan said the public system would struggle to keep up with excess demand.

"They're removing a set of services which are very well established with really good clinicians and really good outcomes because of their particular set of beliefs," he said.

"The public hospitals are so stressed and so burdened that the wards are always busy.

" This is pretty upsetting. "

Health Minister Ryan Park said he was aware of the community's concerns, but the state government did not have the power to intervene in private sales.

"We don't decide what services a private hospital can and can't and won't be delivering," he told ABC Newcastle Breakfast.

"What we're looking at there is whether a particular organisation is fit and proper to hold a health licence," Minister Park said.

"We're looking at any gaps and how those gaps might be resolved."

The Code of Ethical Standards for Catholic Health and Aged Care states that procedures which assist the "marital act to achieve its purpose" are morally permissible, but discourages in-vitro fertilisation, labelling it "contrary to respect for human life in its origins".

"Catholic healthcare facilities should not engage in procedures that intentionally and in themselves damage or destroy an embryo," the code reads.

The code of ethics also states Catholic facilities should not provide or refer for abortions, labelling the practice "morally wrong".

Concerns have been raised over the impact on IVF services. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

Hunter IVF offers services adjacent to Newcastle Private and has traditionally completed egg collections in the hospital's operating theatres.

In a statement, clinical director Andrew Hedges said the organisation is having conversations with a number of other private hospitals about arrangements for hospital-based procedures.

"Calvary Health Care does not have access to our laboratory, and its decisions about hospital services do not affect our laboratory operations or the safe storage of patients' eggs," the statement read.

Calvary already runs the Calvary Mater Hospital in Newcastle, one of the largest cancer hospitals in the state outside Sydney.

In a statement, Calvary said the acquisitions would provide "greater stability" for the hospitals, their employees and the community.

It said the majority of services would be retained.

title: It was a 90s anthem that made millions from a 'stolen' sweet lullaby
text:
It was a song used by Sony, Porsche and SBS.

But the Solomon Islander who sang it barely saw a cent.

Today, a battle for recognition – and royalties – has begun.

Elen Kasi, the one surviving daughter of Afunakwa ( )

Elen Kasi has seen a lot in her 75 years. But these days, her eyes are starting to fail her.

Elen Kasi needs a walking stick these days. ( )

Age is catching up and her memory's a little patchy. But on this fact her mind is crystal clear.

Elen holding Deep Forrest's self-titiled first album. ( )

"After she sung, they paid her $2," she said.

"Whenever I hear her song, I have a sense of pride that it's her. But to this date, I just want to be compensated on behalf of my mum."

A Sweet Lullaby

Elen's mother is Afunakwa.

For most people that means nothing.

Even in her home country, Solomon Islands, she's barely known.

Afunakwa died in 1987 and there are no photos of her.

But her voice has been heard by millions around the world.

Afunakwa sang a lullaby called Rorogwela, recorded in 1969 in the Solomon Islands region of Baegu and used in massive 1990s hit song Sweet Lullaby, by French group Deep Forest.

But crucially, the man who recorded Afunakwa – the man who gave her $2 – says he never gave Deep Forest permission to use the lullaby.

Deep Forest's Sweet Lullaby CD single ( )

The original video for Sweet Lullaby, which was later replaced, depicted an African woman and her child in a desert scene. ( )

For decades Afunakwa was uncredited and the people of Baegu in Solomon Islands never mentioned.

The lullaby was instead attributed to African tribes, with the original music video showing an African woman and her son.

The people of Baegu say it's simple.

They say the song was stolen.

And today, they want answers.

Number one in Australia

At the time, it was a type of music that had not been heard.

The French duo behind Deep Forest, Eric Mouquet and Michel Sanchez, often referred to it as "ethnic electronica" – mixing world music melodies or chants with electronic dance music.

In Australia, Deep Forest's popularity went to another level.

Eric Mouquet and Michel Sanchez, better known as French duo Deep Forest ( )

Sweet Lullaby was the lead single that helped propel Deep Forest's 1992 album to number one in Australia, the only country where that happened.

The album went on sell an estimated 3.5 million copies worldwide.

Sweet Lullaby was a marketer's dream, with brands including Sony, Coca-Cola and Porsche using it to promote their products.

The song made millions through CD sales and licensing and was used in films and viral videos.

Loading...

Sweet Lullaby remains popular today, with more than 50 million streams. Deep Forest is still touring and still playing the song.

In the music industry, samples such as Afunakwa's have to be cleared for use, with the original artist generally receiving royalties or a set payment.

Afunakwa and her family were never asked.

They received nothing.

John Jack, Afunakwa's grandson. ( )

"These people have stolen what belongs to us. They mixed it into something else [and] it's completely lost its meaning," Afunakwa's grandson John Jack said.

A lullaby for an orphan

Baegu, in the Malaita province of Solomon Islands, is incredibly isolated.

There's no mobile phone reception and no internet.

There are no roads in the area the ABC visited, and the only way in is by boat.

The only way in and out of the area is by boat. ( )

A wider map showing where Baegu sits in the world. ( )

A young girl in Baegu pokes her head through a door. ( )

Children in Baegu learn about the significance of lullabies. ( )

But the people here tend to like the isolation.

The kids play soccer and run around.

The adults garden, fish and tell stories.

And they sing – a cultural practice that's been passed on for centuries.

Loading...

"Lullabies are very important to us," 70-year-old Theresa Tafili says.

"My mum knew how to sing and she passed it on to me, and now my daughters know.

"When there's a cultural celebration or a girl gets married, you'll hear a song composed."

Theresa is considered the custodian of Baegu's lullabies, what they call roiroas.

She says Rorogwela, the lullaby used by Deep Forest, has significant cultural meaning.

"It's a song for an orphan," she says.

"In the song, the eldest son is looking after his younger sibling.

"The parents passed away. There was no-one who could help them to look after the child."

Theresa says the lullaby used by Deep Forest has significant cultural meaning. ( ) ]

Theresa Tafili is the considered the custodian of Baegu's lullabies. ( )

Theresa says she remembers the day a "white man" came to Baegu almost 60 years ago to record her relative, Afunakwa, sing it.

That man was Swiss ethnomusicologist Hugo Zemp.

Zemp's recording, intended as a field recording for cultural purposes, was included on a UNESCO collection (now available for streaming) found by Deep Forest in a Paris record store and used in Sweet Lullaby.

Hugo Zemp was an ethnomusicologist, a person who studies music as a reflection of culture. ( ) ]

The album spotted by Deep Forest in a Paris record store. ( )

And this is where the story gets even murkier.

'Pay back your profits'

Zemp died in January at 88.

But he maintained until his death that he never gave Deep Forrest permission to use the recording of Afunakwa used in Sweet Lullaby.

In a 1996 letter to Deep Forest, he wrote:

"You usurped my name in declaring that your enterprise had my support," he said.

"The piece which you entitled 'Sweet Lullaby' … you improperly credited as your composition, stealing the tune which belongs to the Baegu people of Malaita.

"[And] stealing the voice of the singer, Afunakwa."

Deep Forest, today, contests this version of events.

Eric Mouquet, the one remaining member of Deep Forest. ( )

In a statement to the ABC, the group's remaining member, Eric Mouquet, said he provided a list of samples and recordings used in the first Deep Forest album, including Sweet Lullaby, to the record's producers.

He said it was wrong to assume that "everything was decided by the musicians who created the final arrangement".

Mouquet told the ABC French producer Dan Lacksman, the only one of three producers still alive, was "responsible for obtaining the permissions necessary".

In a statement to the ABC, Lacksman said he was only responsible for providing "the recording studio".

He said "permissions and administrative tasks" were the responsibility of now-defunct record label Celine Music, now owned by Sony Music in France.

Sony did not respond to the ABC's request for comment.

Hugo Zemp, pictured here in Solomon Islands, maintained that he never gave permission for the lullaby to be used. ( )

For Zemp, the resolution was simple:

"It is time to put your good words into action and pay back part of your profits to the real owners of this music," he wrote.

Now, 34 years after Sweet Lullaby's release, an unlikely source is doing just that.

Recouping royalties

Baegu man Celsus Talifilu describes it as a "family thing".

His father was village chief in Baegu when the recording of Afunakwa was made by Zemp.

"It is very close to my heart," he said.

Celsus Talifilu, a community leader from Baegu, says he has long wanted proper recognition for the song. ( )

The Baegu area has many artificial islands, all part of its isolation. ( )

Talifilu, now special advisor to the Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale, heard the story of Afunakwa many times growing up.

He's made it a personal mission to right what he calls a terrible wrong.

"As a Baegu man, I'm very honoured and proud of something [like this lullaby] comes from my place," he said.

“But there should have been that respect given to where the song came from."

Celsus says the people of Baegu deserve more recognition. ( )

At one point, more than a decade ago, he said he spoke to lawyers in the US about pursuing a legal fight against Deep Forest.

But the cost was too great, he said, with most lawyers frightened off by the threat of facing corporate giant Sony, which owns the rights to Deep Forest's former label.

So when he received a call out of the blue from an Australian chasing information about Afunakwa, his ears pricked up.

That man was Sydney-based electronic music producer Matt Singmin.

Matt Singmin discovered the 'murky' history of the song and decided to do something about it. ( )

In 2017, Singmin, whose focus is "meditative electronic music" was a DJ at Sydney yoga events.

He was looking into classic songs of the early 1990s and wanted to remix Sweet Lullaby, so he contacted Deep Forest for permission.

"It was difficult to get them to agree to do a licence," he said.

"So I started looking into the history of the song and discovered there's a somewhat murky history to it.

" I started thinking, 'If I'm going to try and release this track ethically, I may need to take a different approach.' "

Singmin decided to travel to Baegu in 2018 to ask for permission to remix the song himself and documented the experience in a documentary recently released on YouTube.

Matt Singmin travelled to Baegu and released a documentary, Searching For Afunakwa. ( )

Matt Singmin in his Sydney music studio. ( )

He wanted to do more.

"It doesn't feel fair that the people from where the song came, and the original singer and her family, never received anything," he said.

In conjunction with Celsus and Afunakwa's grandsons, Singmin has launched the Afunakwa Foundation, a fund to try and recoup some of the royalties the people of Baegu never received.

“The hope is that some of the people that may have benefited from the lullaby might consider that the right thing to do would be to make a donation," he said.

'Very regrettable', says Deep Forest founder

Deep Forest is in the middle of a European tour, still playing to small but dedicated audiences who have followed the group for more than three decades.

Eric Mouquet, the remaining member of Deep Forest, on tour in Bristol last month. ( )

Deep Forest still plays regularly across Europe. ( )

After originally agreeing to an interview, Mouquet's booking agent said he had "no time left" due to the tour and preferred to write his answers.

In an eight-page statement to the ABC he said it was "very regrettable" Afunakwa was not credited and he "completely understood" why the community might feel "hurt, disappointed or angry".

Deep Forest has since amended its YouTube version of Sweet Lullaby to mention her and Hugo Zemp.

"I don't want this story to become a confrontation between people who share a love for the same music," Mouquet said.

"I am personally open to collaborating with Afunakwa's family and discussing how I can make a positive contribution."

The children of Baegu. ( )

He said audiences still "connected deeply" with the song when he performed it today.

"I think that says something extraordinary about the universal beauty of the original melody and Afunakwa's voice," he said.

As they wait for the next chapter of this story, it's one fact the people Baegu can agree on.

Elen Kasi holding the Deep Forest CD. ( )

You can watch the video version of this story on 7:30 tonight or on The Pacific on ABC iview.

title: Netball blindsided by leak of likely inclusion at Brisbane Olympics
text:
Netball has been blindsided by a leak of its likely inclusion at the Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games.

Media reports by NewsCorp suggest it is "near the top of the list" in priority for the 2032 organising committee, which is permitted to put forward up to six local sports to feature as one-offs at the Games.

Cricket, surf lifesaving, rugby league and lawn bowls are also in the frame.

This would set netball up for a historic Games debut. Despite being part of the Commonwealth Games since 1998, it has tried and failed at least four times to join the Olympic programme previously.

Loading Instagram content

The endorsement is a positive sign, the significance of which is not lost on Netball Australia, who have garnered more than 115,000 signatures on their petition since officially launching a bid to join the Brisbane Games in 2021.

In January, a survey conducted by independent market and social research agency Insightfully, found 66 per cent of Australians support netball's inclusion at the Olympics. It polled 10 points higher than any other sport.

However, key figures at Netball Australia were tight-lipped on Thursday, for fear of speaking out of turn and jeopardising their chances.

Earlier this week, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) revised its timeline for determining which sports and disciplines would make it onto the programme for the Brisbane Games.

In December, the IOC will make recommendations in three different categories: existing disciplines to have automatic inclusion; existing or proposed disciplines that require further assessment; and candidate disciplines eliminated from consideration.

A formal verdict will be handed down in April next year after votes are taken at the IOC session in the Dominican Republic.

Former Australian defender turned-commentator Bianca Chatfield shared her initial reaction with ABC Sport.

"Everyone is really shocked that it's come out and there has been this leak," Chatfield said.

"I was so excited when I saw the news, but then I dug deeper and realised it's not official.

"We're all just holding on with hope that the news is real and that it'll come to fruition next year."

Bianca Chatfield (left) faces New Zealand in the 2013 Constellation Cup. (Getty: Michael Dodge)

Chatfield said the Olympics always felt out of reach as an option for netball, but the sport deserved its chance to shine at the Games.

"It would mean everything to the sport, there's been a lot of work done behind the scenes," she said.

"For the athletes especially it would be a once in a lifetime opportunity to have a crack at an Olympic gold medal.

"The Olympics was just something that we never thought would happen so the fact it's a tangible thing now, we'd all be absolutely stoked to see it happen."

Bianca Chatfield now works as a commentator and presenter in the game. (Getty: Graham Denholm)

The Australian team's recent form sees it on the brink of losing the world number one ranking for the first time since 2013, but that lapse in dominance could perhaps help a greater cause.

The Diamonds missed the Commonwealth Games final for the first time in Glasgow, falling to Jamaica in the semifinals before rallying to claim bronze. They also conceded the Constellation Cup to New Zealand for just the fourth time in 16 series.

"I do think a competitive environment really helps [our Olympic case]," Chatfield said.

"As we're seeing internationally, with the rise of teams like Jamaica and New Zealand, it's not a forgone conclusion that Australia would get the gold."

Federal Minister for Communications and Sport Anika Wells, who is also vice chair on the board of the Brisbane 2032 committee, pledged her support at the Queensland Media Club on Thursday.

She also told ABC Sport that it was feasible that multiple team sports like cricket and netball could be selected, despite there being pressure to remain inside the overall 10,500 athlete quota.

Sports Minister Anika Wells fronts the media. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"Today I am publicly committing my support to netball as part of Brisbane 2032," Wells said.

"Netball is quintessentially Australian and the leading team sport for women and girls here and across our region.

"It connects communities, it creates leaders, it builds confidence and inspires dreams.

"It would be a massive moment for the million little girls and women, and increasingly men and boys, who pull on their netball bibs and get out to play."

Former Diamond Kathryn Harby-Williams is the CEO at ANPA. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Chief executive of the Australian Netball Players' Association Kathryn Harby-Williams said the athletes welcomed the news.

"It would be an incredible opportunity for the athletes if it is true, to compete at one of the biggest sports events in the world," Harby-Williams told ABC Sport.

Meanwhile, a Netball Australia spokesperson said it would follow due process.

"We are focused on putting our best foot forward with the Brisbane 2032 Organising Committee and the IOC and we respect their processes," a statement read.

"We will continue to advocate for netball and our incredible community across the globe.

"There are countless Australian netball players who dream of one day becoming an Olympian and we believe Brisbane 2032 would be the perfect stage for those dreams."

title: Albanese's Caribbean trip is no holiday as he faces grilling over economy
text:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

Anthony Albanese has been searching for a reason to justify the optics of trading Canberra for the Caribbean the same week the Reserve Bank was expected to lift rates again.

A personal plea from King Charles locked in his travel to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM). It was a summit he could have missed, but he assured the public it was a good opportunity for a chat with his UK counterpart Andy Burnham.

The "enormous pressure" caused by the almost doubled arrivals of UK backpackers was at the top of the list, as the government continues to hunt for ways to reduce net-overseas migration.

There was no sign that Albanese was in a tropical paradise as he addressed media. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Albanese wants to tighten the rules under the Morrison-era free trade deal that exempted British travellers from regional and rural work. He did not secure that this week.

The issue was almost absent from the UK prime minister's readout, beyond mention of "the importance of ensuring opportunities for young people both at home and abroad". It didn't make Albanese's readout either.

In a room that bared more of a resemblance to a school portable than a tropical island getaway, Albanese said talks were "very constructive" and insisted there were options officials were going to canvas further.

The failure to come home with a deal will only fuel the Coalition's criticisms of the trip at a time when so many Australians are feeling hip-pocket pain.

The prime minister's travel schedule over the coming weeks isn't letting up either. He'll head to the Türkiye resort town of Antalya for COP31, before he stops in the Philippines and China. Another expected trip to the United States for the G20 in Miami is also on the agenda for December.

Anthony Albanese was far away from home but couldn’t dodge interest rate questions. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

In full view of cameras, Albanese mentioned questions from reporters to King Charles about why he thought it was important to attend CHOGM.

"Oh God, it's all my fault, oh no," the King replied.

One of Albanese's more flimsy rules (he applies it when it suits him) is not to address domestic issues abroad. But on this trip, he had no choice but to defend his economic record when asked about it both ahead of, and after, the central bank lifted rates to an 18-year high.

Engaging with the international community was part of making our economy stronger, he argued.

Loading...

Shifting tides and seats in parliament

Half a world away, a defeated-looking treasurer was left to take the impact of the fifth rate hike this year.

Jim Chalmers again shifted the blame for persistently high inflation. The message was complicated by the Reserve Bank, which pointed out the hike was to deal with "domestic capacity pressures".

Basically, Governor Michele Bullock said it's not that the oil shock from the Middle East war wasn't a contributing factor, but things at home hadn't helped matters either.

Loading...

Chalmers is facing calls to tighten the budget belt as the expenditure review committee meets in the lead up to the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher stressed they were looking for savings "across the board" while at the same time pointing the finger at the Coalition for blocking some savings measures in the Senate.

But on the question of net savings — when savings are greater than the sum of spending — the government was non-committal.

Interest rates are the only lever the central bank has to reduce inflation. It's why the prime minister called it a blunt instrument as he put both physical and metaphorical distance between himself and the decision.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

Bullock made it clear that a slowdown in economic growth was on the way. We aren't heading for a recession, but it's sure going to feel like one, she warned.

For a government that's already struggling with a mid-term slump, the perception that nothing is getting better is another problem it'll have to overcome. And quick.

Chalmers conceded last week a bit of paint had been chipped off after the budget. This week he was not only defending his record, but also whether he should keep his job.

"I'm wondering whether you've given any thought to stepping aside and giving someone else a go," a reporter asked.

"No," Chalmers said.

If Albanese follows the pattern of last term, there will be a frontbench refresh at some point; much of the cabinet has been around since the last time rates were this high, back in the Rudd era.

The treasurer has been defending his economic record after the Reserve Bank lifted rates to an 18-year high. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Speaking of shuffling around, one person looking to switch houses is Nationals leader Matt Canavan. He has put his hand up to leave the Senate and seek pre-selection for the Central Queensland seat of Capricornia after Michelle Landry announced her retirement.

As resident numbers man Casey Briggs wrote this week, the move is a risk. He'll face a fight from One Nation to win the seat. But if recent opinion polls are to be believed, he is in an uphill battle to retain his Senate spot anyway.

Digital safety laws praised and pulled apart

In a courtroom down the road from Parliament House in Canberra, Anika Wells this week listened to part of the first day of a challenge to the government's social media laws.

Reddit and the advocacy group Digital Freedom Project are both asking the High Court to throw out the laws, arguing the ban is unconstitutional because it excludes young people from civic engagement.

High Court to hear social media ban challenge Australia's world-first social media ban for users under 16 will face its first major legal challenge in the High Court today, nearly a year after taking effect.

The two teens who were named co-plaintiffs in the original filing against the Commonwealth were removed from the case over concerns they would be held personally liable for legal costs should the matter fail.

Nearly five million social media accounts have been blocked since the laws came into force last December, and Reddit has questioned the speed at which the laws were passed through parliament. Wells, who took questions outside the courtroom, noted she wasn't the communications minister at the time.

Around the same time in Antigua, Andy Burnham was congratulating Albanese on being a real leader in the online safety space.

Next week, the government's digital duty of care laws will come under further scrutiny as a Senate inquiry kicks off.

It's legislation both Albanese and Wells would love off their to-do list by the time parliament rises for the end of the year.

title: Woman dies from leptospirosis after hunting near Top End billabong
text:
A woman has died after contracting leptospirosis while hunting near a billabong in a remote Top End community.

The patient, aged in her 30s who also had underlying health conditions, developed a "rapid infection" from the serious bacterial illness and died at Royal Darwin Hospital a week ago.

The exact location where the woman contracted leptospirosis or how long she had been unwell remains unclear.

The ABC understands the patient was one of four confirmed cases admitted to Royal Darwin Hospital's intensive care unit in recent months.

The three others have since been discharged.

NT health has confirmed 11 people have contracted the illness so far in 2026, up from six recorded cases in the Territory last year.

Authorities are urging people to take extra care around NT waterways.

Leptospirosis is a serious bacterial infection which can be spread from water, mud or soil contaminated by infected animal urine, mostly after flooding events.

Leptospira bacteria can be picked up through cuts to the skin or splashes to the eyes, nose or mouth, and causes symptoms including sudden fevers, severe muscle pain and bloodshot eyes.

Last month, NT authorities issued a public health alert for the bacterial infection, and identified areas around Fogg Dam, Harrison Dam, Gunbalanya, Finniss River, Tipperary Station, rural Darwin, Katherine and Arnhem Land as places with an increased risk.

People who hunt, muster, bushwalk or interact with animals are being warned to take extra precautions including avoiding wading through potentially contaminated water, covering open wounds and wearing protective clothing.

Early diagnosis and treatment of the illness is critical, with NT Health urging anyone with symptoms to seek urgent medical attention.

title: Stock already being cleared as David Jones goes into administration
text:
David Jones customers have rushed to spend gift cards hours after news broke the retailer's future was in serious jeopardy.

The iconic 188-year-old department store chain entered voluntary administration and receivership this morning.

At the David Jones store inside the Highpoint Shopping Centre in Melbourne's west, some shelves were short of stock, while others were due to be cleared by staff.

Shoppers had also come to redeem gift cards.

Pauline Ricotta visited the David Jones store at Highpoint Shopping Centre to redeem a gift card. (ABC News: Loretta Florance)

"The staff were saying that it's really busy today, but it's very sombre," shopper Pauline Ricotta said.

Ms Ricotta said she had come into the store to spend a $300 gift card she had had for a year.

Another shopper, Sonya, said she wanted to use $450 worth of gift cards before it was too late.

"I've always found these [suburban] DJs, they don't really have as much stock as the city or Chadstone, but it's the closest one to home, so I quickly came in," she said.

She said she had planned to wait until Black Friday sales, but came to the store after the news broke.

"I bought a couple of things, things that I probably wouldn't have spent that amount of money on if I was paying for it," she said.

"It was better than having to go dollar for dollar with the voucher or lose it completely as an unsecured creditor if that's what the administrators decide to do."

'If you have a gift card, go now'

Consumer Policy Research Centre chief executive Erin Turner encouraged people with outstanding gift cards to go into David Jones stores and spend them as soon as they can.

The outlook for shoppers as David Jones placed in receivership Here's what the experts say shoppers should consider to avoid a Christmas nightmare.

"If you have a gift card, go now," Ms Turner said.

"You have a small window where you can guarantee you can use it.

"While the company is in administration [and receivership], they're looking closely at the books, but they've confirmed they'll continue trading. This means the doors are still open.

"We don't know what's going to happen after this period of looking closely at the books. The company could remain open, it could wind up, or it might just close local stores near you that make using a gift card less smooth and easy.

" Definitely do not buy another gift card. "

She warned if David Jones was wound up, people may lose the money attached to gift cards because they would be treated as unsecured creditors and placed behind others the business was in debt to.

Anyone with David Jones rewards points should also try to spend them quickly, she said.

Applications for new David Jones credit cards have been stopped by the finance company that provides them, Latitude.

In a statement, a Latitude spokesperson said existing cardholders were not affected and could continue using their card.

Business as usual on David Jones website

There was little sign of the financial problems plaguing David Jones on its website today, where ads for perfume and make-up brands, beauty gift cards and members' sales were prominently advertised along with a large range of Christmas gifts.

The David Jones website appeared to be trading as usual at lunchtime on Thursday. (ABC News)

Ms Turner recommended shoppers go to a physical store rather than shopping online.

"It's very likely that if you buy something online today, you will still receive it, but there's a chance that you might not or a chance there'll be delays or issues," she said.

Gary Mortimer says customers may face extra conditions on gift cards. (Supplied: Gary Mortimer)

Queensland University of Technology retail expert Gary Mortimer said receivers would have to work out how to treat gift cards and rewards points, and they could come with new conditions.

"I recall that Barbeques Galore, for example, when they went into administration, the administrator honoured gift cards, but it required a subsequent purchase on top of the gift card amount," Professor Mortimer said.

"If you had a $100 gift card, you had to spend $200 in store to redeem that $100."

When retailer Dick Smith went into receivership in 2016, customers who put down deposits on items or had gift vouchers did not get their money back or have them honoured.

Consumer advocates, including Ms Turner, have argued funds from gift cards should be stored in trust to ensure people do not lose their money when a business goes belly up.

title: How the Wegovy pill compares to weight-loss injections
text:
A new tablet version of Wegovy, a peptide used to help people lose weight, has been approved for the first time in Australia.

Until now, the best-known medicines in this group (semaglutide, sold as Wegovy or Ozempic, and tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro), have generally required weekly injections. The new daily tablet offers another option for people who would prefer not to (or can't) inject themselves.

But how does it work? And will swallowing a pill make weight loss easier, cheaper or safer?

What are Wegovy pills, and what's changed?

Wegovy contains semaglutide, a medicine that copies the action of a naturally occurring hormone called glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1). This hormone helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and digestion.

On Tuesday, Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) registered four strengths of Wegovy tablets: 1.5mg, 4mg, 9mg and 25mg.

This makes it the first GLP-1 medicine approved in Australia in tablet form specifically for weight management.

Semaglutide's like Wegovy contain a hormone that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and digestion. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

How do the tablets work, and who are they for?

Semaglutide acts on the brain and digestive system. It reduces hunger, increases feelings of fullness and slows how quickly food leaves the stomach. This can help people feel satisfied with smaller meals and reduce how often they feel hungry.

The medicine is intended for adults living with obesity, or people who are overweight and have other weight-related health conditions. It may also be prescribed to some people with heart (cardiovascular) disease to reduce their risk of serious heart problems, such as heart attack or stroke.

These medicines are not intended as a quick fix for people wanting to lose a few kilograms. They are prescription treatments that should be considered as part of a person's broader health needs, with guidance from a health-care professional.

How do the pills compare to injections?

The Wegovy tablet must be taken daily, on an empty stomach with a small amount of water, with a 30-minute wait before you eat or drink anything other than water. They contain a special absorption aid to pass through stomach acid, to allow it to be absorbed properly and work effectively.

In contrast, the injection can be done any time of day, once weekly, with or without food.

Weight-loss drug manufacturers under fire for 'unethical' ads Two pharmaceutical giants have recently launched advertisements directing people towards their doctor for weight loss. Some experts warn this type of advertising may affect public health messaging.

Both formats work to make you stay fuller faster, and trials showed similar gastrointestinal effects especially when first starting.

Overall, they show similar rates of weight loss, with the tablet showing a 14 per cent body weight loss over 64–68 weeks, and the injection showing a 15 per cent weight reduction. However, the pill's effectiveness relies on people remembering to take it each day and not eat or drink within half an hour of the dose, rather than just remembering to inject the drug once a week.

What are the risks?

Common side effects — affecting around 80 per cent of patients — include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, indigestion and constipation.

Less common, but more serious side effects include kidney injury, pancreatitis and gallbladder problems.

Higher doses make negative side effects more severe. With a tablet, it's important for people to know that, just as for an injection, doubling up their dose won't encourage faster results and could cause harm.

Why experts are worried about the latest peptides trend The latest wellness craze to take social media by storm is fuelling a growing grey market of injectable peptides in Australia, and it has experts worried.

Doctor appointments are short, meaning they sometimes lack proper screening for eating disorders, body image or other psychological issues. Previous research has also highlighted a link between suicidal thoughts and GLP-1 use. So unless these issues are discussed in appointments, it could lead to negative outcomes for patients.

An oral tablet may be easier for people who don't like needles or have trouble using them, and could reduce potential injection-related injuries. Recently, needle and syringe programs have been overwhelmed with demand for needles used for GLP-1s and other peptides.

When will pills be available, and what will they cost?

The TGA approval doesn't mean you can walk into your doctor and get a script today.

Before Wegovy tablets hit the shelves, the TGA will complete a final review of packaging and production, as well as retail pricing. Novo Nordisk, the company that manufactures Wegovy, aims to have tablets available in Australia by the end of the year.

It is also important to distinguish TGA approval from Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) listing. TGA approval means a medicine can be prescribed for its approved uses. PBS listing means the government subsidises its cost. Wegovy is not currently subsidised through the PBS for weight management, meaning patients should expect to pay the full price.

Official pricing hasn't been released yet. However, the weekly injection costs A$250–$450 a month and the pill's out-of-pocket costs are likely to be similar.

Is this a 'magic pill'?

This pill isn't meant to be used by itself. The TGA has approved Wegovy tablets to use alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.

It's also important to follow prescriber guidelines, eat nutritious food, and do weight training to help avoid muscle loss.

This is why "lifestyle prescribing" should accompany any weight-loss drugs, which means GPs should also make a clear plan with patients to encourage healthy eating and regular exercise, alongside weight-loss medications.

This matters because when people lose weight quickly, some of what they lose is lean muscle, not just body fat.

Secondly, the weight can come back if you stop taking Wegovy without having changed your lifestyle. Follow-up research with participants has found people regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost within a year of stopping these medications.

Kimberley Akrigg is a PhD candidate, Samuel Cornell is a research fellow and Timothy Platkowski is a senior research fellow. All work in the School of Public Health at the University of Queensland. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

title: Woodside to axe 500 jobs, sparking fears for WA workers
text:
Gas giant Woodside Energy has announced it will axe at least 500 jobs from its global workforce as part of plans to cut costs by $550 million a year from 2028.

The planned job cuts equate to about 10 per cent of its workforce, but it is not clear how many of these will come from its extensive LNG operations in Australia, primarily centred off Western Australia's coast.

About 80 per cent of Woodside's workforce is based in Australia, with the vast majority stationed in WA, fuelling fears the announcement will result in job losses for West Australians.

Woodside's $17 billion Scarborough development is located in the Carnarvon Basin off the Pilbara coast. (ABC News)

The restructure was announced today as part of a broader strategy to increase returns to investors, with Woodside chief executive Liz Westcott singling out the Scarborough gas project as one of the ventures that would massively bolster the company's finances for years to come.

She said the project, located about 375 kilometres off WA's Pilbara coast, was "80 per cent complete" and just weeks away from shipping its first LNG cargo.

Woodside approval paves the way for the mother of all climate battles When all the hype and the fury are stripped away, the decision to extend the life of the gigantic North West Shelf LNG plant boils down to one thing — enabling the Browse gas project off the Kimberley coast.

The North West Shelf, which was controversially given the green light to keep operating until 2070, was also singled out as a key project in the company's future plans.

The decision to extend the life of the gigantic gas plant is seen as the key to enabling the contentious Browse gas project off the Kimberley coast.

Despite facing many hurdles to developing Browse, Woodside identifies the gas fields as a "growth option" as part of its long-term strategy, describing it as "one of Australia's largest undeveloped resources".

Latest blow

The cuts are the latest blow to the state's resources sector following a series of lay-offs in the iron ore industry this year.

BHP to cut hundreds of jobs Mining giant BHP confirms job cuts at its iron ore operations in Western Australia.

In June, Gina Rinehart's Hancock Iron Ore confirmed job cuts at its Roy Hill operations.

The miner did not reveal the extent of the job losses, but reports suggested they were in the hundreds.

In October, BHP announced it would axe up to 300 jobs across its WA iron ore operations in the Pilbara.

A company spokesperson said the changes were necessary so BHP could continue to "make a significant contribution" to the region and the state.

Treasurer 'disappointed'

WA Treasurer Rita Saffioti said she was "very disappointed" about the job cuts, adding her government would continue "to bat for gas" as a key transition fuel for the state.

WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti is calling on Australia to keep backing the gas sector and gas projects. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

She said Australia needed to make “key decisions” about whether the country supported resources and gas projects.

“On any given day there are people saying that we shouldn’t support gas projects, and then on other given days people are saying that we want to make sure we get strong employment,” Ms Saffioti said.

"We are a resources state, gas is an integral part of our energy supply, and let's keep supporting the gas sector as part of our overall economic vision."

WA Greens spokesperson Sophie McNeill said the cutbacks were "proof" Woodside was a fossil fuels company "in decline", and it should not be allowed to drill for gas at Scott Reef as part of its Browse project.

'Strong focus' on shareholder value

Resources analyst Peter Strachan said Woodside was certainly not a company in decline, and had "money falling into its coffers" with high oil prices linked to the Iran war.

He described the changes as Ms Westcott — who was appointed as permanent CEO in March this year — "stamping her authority over the organisation" with a "very strong focus" on shareholder value.

Peter Strachan says Woodside is not a company in decline. (Supplied: Peter Strachan)

Mr Strachan did not believe the cuts were imminent, suspecting action would be taken over the next six months and would include new energy projects involving hydrogen and ammonia, as well as the Scarborough project.

"They will be able to turn around and say the project people are no longer needed and can either redeploy them, or they are sort of [surplus to requirements]," he said.

"Since Woodside has decided to phase down its exposure to ammonia, there might be people working on that project that are no longer needed going forward."

title: Swans 'need to be better' as club culture comes under spotlight again
text:
Sydney Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich admits the embattled AFL club has a "long way to go" as it grapples with a culture problem that has been exacerbated by Tom Papley allegedly driving under the influence of drugs.

Papley, a high-profile forward and one of the team's most experienced players, allegedly returned a positive roadside test for methylamphetamine on Monday and will appear in court this month for driving with a suspended licence.

If Papley's second sample is positive, the 216-gamer is likely to face an AFL penalty separate from any legal sanction.

Pavlich spoke briefly to reporters outside the club headquarters in Moore Park today, conceding the Swans had again let down the football community.

"We're bitterly disappointed that we're here talking about this today," Pavlich said.

"We're really disappointed in Tom himself. We voiced that pretty directly to him yesterday.

"We apologise unreservedly to our members, fans and corporate partners.

"We've let them down again. We must be better.

"It's a really disappointing time for the footy club, but given this is a police matter, we cannot make any further comment."

Tom Papley (centre) allegedly returned a positive roadside test for methylamphetamine on Monday. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Papley's looming court appearance comes after the Swans suspended five players for breaching club behavioural standards last August.

Vice-captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were stood down for the remainder of the AFL season and missed the finals.

"We're looking at that right now," Pavlich said, when asked if the Swans had a culture problem.

"We've been identifying that over the last eight weeks.

"We've started some deep work on that with our AFL men's department, independent advisers helping us through that.

"These are the questions we are asking ourselves right now and asking our players."

Pavlich added "we need to be better".

"This is not something that anyone is stopping short of, knowing that we've got a long way to go," he said.

"We've got some deep work to do to understand how we can get better."

Second test results to take weeks

Papley was pulled over by police in Sydney's Centennial Park on Monday for random testing.

He was subjected to a roadside drug test, with checks revealing his licence was suspended due to non-payment of a parking fine.

A secondary sample of oral fluid was taken for further analysis, with the results from the second test expected to take at least four weeks.

Papley was issued a 24-hour driving prohibition and will appear before Waverley Local Court on November 26.

The 30-year-old's test result has overshadowed a landmark week for the Swans, who on Sunday will host their first AFLW home final at Henson Park.

No update on hotel incident

Meanwhile, Victoria Police are yet to provide an update on an investigation into sexual assault allegations at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel following a round 23 AFL game.

Detectives in early September travelled to NSW to interview a 30-year-old Maroubra man, a 25-year-old Paddington man and two Randwick men aged 25 and 26.

It is understood the men interviewed were Heeney, Warner, Jordon and Blakey.

No charges have been laid. AAP is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the suspended players.

Bice is no longer a person of interest for police, while Blakey departed the Swans during last month's trade period to join North Melbourne.

title: Big batteries ready to power one-third of ACT for hours if needed
text:
The largest battery energy storage system in Canberra's history is online, with the ACT government saying the batteries could power one-third of Canberra's electricity needs for two hours in times of peak demand.

The Williamsdale site, south of Tuggeranong, has 136 Tesla Megapack 2 batteries and connects to the electricity grid, absorbing excess energy in times of low demand, before returning it to the grid when demand is high.

The project is a partnership between the government and private company Eku Energy, which designed, built and owns the 250-megawatt capacity batteries.

The timeline to complete the project blew out twice after its delivery was projected to be in 2025, then later extended to early in 2026, which was also not realised.

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr (centre) says he believes the project will be cost-positive for the ACT government. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr said as part of the operating agreement, the government would pay Eku Energy a support charge of $368 million in instalments across 15 years.

The government is entitled to 50 per cent of the battery's net revenue, which it earns when energy is sold back to the grid.

Mr Barr said he expected the project to become revenue-positive.

"So, the territory makes a contribution, then receives more in its share of the revenue," he said.

"We are building this technology for households, small business, for our hospitals, for our schools, for our universities, for all of the industrial output that occurs in Canberra ... data centres are part of that," Mr Barr said.

"That's why this is such a good project for the ACT."

How does it work?

The batteries are located in Williamsdale in the ACT's south. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

Eku Energy policy director Rachel Rundle explained that the battery system was connected to Evoenergy's infrastructure.

"Essentially they're plugged into the electricity network," she said.

"They are always on … [and] because they're always on, they soak up all of the excess energy that is in the network.

Eku Energy policy director Rachel Rundle said she expected the system would sell energy back to the grid each day. (Supplied)

"Lots of that excess energy comes from the great wind and solar resources that we have in Australia.

"It stores and holds onto that energy for a number of hours.

"And then when that demand picks up … say, on a hot evening night or when there's a lot of industrial processing, the battery discharges that energy back into the grid, helping meet that peak demand and reducing the strain on the network."

Ms Rundle said it could quickly store up to 500-megawatt hours and then discharge that amount each day.

Eku Energy chief operating officer Tom Best said there were no promises that the system would put downward pressure on Canberra household electricity bills.

title: Study finds one third of infants diagnosed with peanut allergy can eat nuts
text:
More than one third of babies thought to have a peanut allergy may actually be able to safely eat nuts, according to a new study.

Researchers say the study could change the way the healthcare system approaches infant food allergies and lead to many children having their allergy diagnosis removed.

The research was led by the Murdoch Children's Research Institute and the National Allergy Centre of Excellence (NACE) in partnership with 10 paediatric public hospitals across Australia.

Researchers found 35 per cent of infants with a previous reaction to peanut and a positive allergy test did not react to an oral food challenge.

Researchers say peanut allergies affect about one in 30 children in Australia. (Adobe Stock)

NACE Director Kirsten Perrett said the number of children who did not react to peanut during a supervised food challenge was "surprising".

"These were children that had had a history of reactions when they were introduced to peanuts and they'd had a positive test, be it a skin prick test or a blood test," Professor Perrett told ABC News Breakfast.

"Our results show that clinical history and allergy testing alone were not enough to accurately diagnose peanut allergy in many cases.

"A supervised oral food challenge should be routinely considered to confirm the diagnosis before an infant starts oral immunotherapy."

Kirsten Perrett leads the ADAPT program at Monash Children's Research Institute. (Supplied)

Melbourne School of Public Health biostatistics professor Lyle Gurrin, who was not involved in the research, said he was not surprised that the figure reported in the research was so high.

"A lot of people think their children are allergic when they're probably not, so I think this paper is good from that point of view that it's encouraging people to seek proper advice," he said.

"I'm not surprised that a large proportion of these infants didn't return a positive result in an oral food challenge."

The study involved 1,275 infants under 18 months of age at hospitals in Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia and Western Australia.

The findings emerged from the ADAPT Peanut Oral Immunotherapy Program hosted by the Murdoch Children's Research Institute, which required infants to undergo a food challenge before starting treatment.

The program exposed children to small, daily doses of peanut to build tolerance.

Hopes to expand study to cashews

Victorian couple Leah and Jake introduced their infant son Arthur to peanuts when he was five months old.

They said the reaction was instant, with his face turning red and hives appearing on his shoulders and under his nose.

Leah and Jake with baby Arthur who ws initially diagnosed with a peanut allergy. (Supplied)

The boy was referred to the ADAPT program but then tolerated the supervised oral food challenge and had his allergy diagnosis removed.

"It's a huge relief knowing Arthur can tolerate peanut and we can move forward without the uncertainty of managing a suspected allergy," Leah said.

" Having the opportunity to find out he could tolerate peanuts has made a real difference to our family. "

Arthur had a reaction to peanuts when he first tried them, leading to an allergy diagnosis. (Supplied)

Professor Perrett said it was hoped the research would make the process of identifying food allergies more accurate for parents like Leah and Jake.

"With peanut allergy one of the most common childhood food allergies, it's particularly important that we have an accurate diagnosis when a baby first shows signs of a possible peanut allergy," she said.

"We want to reduce the burden of food allergy for children and their families, and the ADAPT Program is a step in this direction."

Professor Gurrin said the research did not necessarily mean it would become easier for GPs to better diagnose a child with a peanut allergy.

He said oral food challenges still need to be carried out under appropriate conditions.

"You can't really do that in a GP surgery or a child maternal health clinic," he said.

"You need all the material and the broader understanding to be able to assist the child who is having a reaction, whether it be mild or right through to anaphylaxis."

Professor Perrett said NACE was hoping to expand the ADAPT program to cover cashew allergy, which was almost as prevalent as peanut allergy.

However, Professor Perrett advised parents not to conduct an oral food challenge at home, warning that 12 per cent of infants with a peanut allergy had a potentially-life threatening anaphylactic response.

Kuniko has maintained a perfect strike rate at its Commonwealth-Silica Hill project 100 kilometres north of Orange in central New South Wales, with all 11 diamond holes from a two-phase, 2731-metre drilling program successfully intersecting gold-silver mineralisation. The company’s latest five-hole, 1492-metre campaign was designed to follow up a spectacular discovery made during phase one drilling and appears to have successfully extended the mineralised system, with step-out holes stretching the known mineralisation by 60m down-dip and 40m up-dip, demonstrating a mineralised extent of roughly 100m. The results are expected to feed into an updated mineral resource estimate slated for December this year. Kuniko’s Commonwealth-Silica Hill project in NSW’s prolific Lachlan Fold Belt. The highlight from the new batch of assays was a 16.3-metre hit grading 1.56 grams per tonne (g/t) gold equivalent from a downhole depth of 75.7m, featuring a higher-grade core of 11.95m at 1.95g/t gold equivalent. This hosted two richer veins of 1.1m assaying 5.17g/t gold equivalent and a 0.65-metre section grading a notable 6.23g/t gold equivalent. Other phase-two results included a broad 43-metre intersection grading 0.31g/t gold equivalent, alongside two 30-metre hits running at 0.45g/t and 0.36g/t gold equivalent, respectively. The company’s primary deposits at Commonwealth and Silica Hill have JORC-inferred mineral resource estimates totalling 88,000 ounces of gold and 3.3 million ounces of silver.

‘These results highlight the broader potential of the Commonwealth-Silica Hill system and will inform the updated mineral resource estimate.’ Kuniko Limited managing director Maja McGuire The latest results appear to complement Kuniko’s initial phase one campaign, which delivered a stunning result when a hole, punched 100 metres beyond the previously defined mineralised footprint, intersected a broad 84-metre zone grading 0.6g/t gold and 123g/t silver. The intercept also contained a 0.5-metre massive sulphide vein grading an eye-watering 27g/t gold and a coffee-spitting 20,603g/t silver, a figure that puts it firmly in bonanza territory, where grades above 1000g/t silver are considered exceptional. Kuniko managing director Maja McGuire said: “The completion of our two diamond drilling campaigns at Commonwealth-Silica Hill represents an important milestone for Kuniko, with all 11 holes intersecting mineralisation and providing substantial new geological and assay information to support our upcoming MRE update later this year. Importantly, we continue to identify opportunities beyond the areas tested by drilling.” The company’s ground sits in the heart of New South Wales’ Lachlan Fold Belt, a tier-one mining jurisdiction often referred to as “elephant country” and host to some of Australia’s largest mineral deposits. The region is seeing a fresh wave of investment as soaring copper prices and a renewed appetite for gold bring the mineral-rich province back into the spotlight. Major operations in the neighbourhood include Newmont’s colossal 39-million-ounce Cadia-Ridgeway mine and Evolution Mining’s Cowal operation. The geology adds another intriguing dimension, with two distinct styles of mineralisation sitting just 200 metres apart: a polymetallic volcanogenic massive sulphide system at the company’s Commonwealth deposit and an epithermal stockwork vein system at Silica Hill. The combination has drawn comparisons with world-class deposits such as Canada’s Eskay Creek, renowned for its exceptionally high-grade precious-metal mineralisation.

With the drills now silent, geophysical interpretation is lighting up the path forward. The company recently deployed downhole electromagnetic (DHEM) probes to hunt for deep, off-hole extensions of conductive sulphides. Integrated gravity, induced polarisation and DHEM surveys have now defined a prospective geophysical trend that stretches for more than 500m to the southeast of the known mineralisation at Silica Hill. The company says significant and untested induced polarisation chargeability anomalies and prospective gravity-low margins have provided a grab bag of additional targets for follow-up exploration. Kuniko appears to be building a district-scale play, with plans advancing for a third phase of drilling in the first quarter of 2027 to test near-resource targets at its Welcome Jack, Walls and Stringers prospects, all set within a kilometre of the existing project resource. Historical drilling at these prospects has already shown promise. A previous hole at Welcome Jack returned 2m at 5.7g/t gold, while drilling at Walls produced a 20-metre intercept grading 0.5g/t gold and 27g/t silver. While its current focus is on the gold-silver potential in NSW, Kuniko also holds a portfolio of battery and critical minerals projects in Norway. These include the Ertelien nickel-copper-cobalt project, which holds a 40-million-tonne resource running 0.25 per cent nickel equivalent, in addition to other cobalt and copper assets aimed at servicing the European energy transition.

With mineralisation hit in every hole to date, Kuniko may have demonstrated it could be onto a significant gold-silver system at Commonwealth-Silica Hill. A resource update is just around the corner and a suite of compelling geophysical and regional targets are lining up for the drill bit. The immediate catalysts are now threefold: final assays, integration of the downhole geophysics and the expected resource update, all of which could help reveal just how big this Lachlan Fold Belt system might be. Alluding to the form of late-blooming rookie Oliver Pascoe, the club’s founding fullback said a vision to deliver premiership glory to the region must be the priority motivator should Grant arrive.

“To understand why he wants to come here – if he wants to come here – is really important because you’ve got players here right now who want to be here,” Campbell said. “They’ll work really hard and put their body on the line for the club. To have him here is great, but I’ve played at clubs and seen other clubs take on players who have no interest in coming to benefit the club, they come for the lifestyle and the money. “That’s being honest and that’s being real, and you want players at the club who … want to succeed and grow as a player and person, but want to see the club succeed as well.”

Grant’s acquisition would, however, provide the Titans with the perfect spine leader to guide the outfit’s blossoming playmakers. New Zealand No.1 Keano Kini (2030), halfback Zane Harrison (2029) and Campbell’s son, five-eighth Jayden (2031), are all secured on long-term deals and a player of Grant’s calibre has the potential to unlock the trio’s capabilities. The retention of Harrison has been crucial, given the Gold Coast’s inability to cement a No.7 since inaugural maestro Scott Prince donned the colours. Loading The 20-year-old was caught in a public contract saga, in which figures as high as $900,000 were reported for his services despite playing just 11 games. Debate on whether he was worth such funds ensued, as did links to the Papua New Guinea Chiefs for 2028.

Nor, the homegrown product said, did the tax-free incentives of the Chiefs. “We’re not allowed to speak to other clubs because we hadn’t hit November 1, so I didn’t have my eyes anywhere else. My love for the Gold Coast is unmatched, so my decision was easy,” Harrison said, whose maiden campaign was ended by a hamstring injury. “It was frustrating at the time, the disrespectful comments coming from other people, but I try to ignore that – I knew my love for the Titans, and that’s all that matters. It just flew over my head.

“My goal is to bring success to this club. I was always going to stay loyal.” Harrison revealed he was in regular contact with Titans minority co-owner Matthew Johns, and had been discussing his game with the Newcastle champion and his brother Andrew Johns “week to week” in a bid to take his craft further. Campbell – who won the Dally M Medal as a No.7 with Cronulla in 2001 – believed Harrison could bring silverware to the city in a way that even Prince, who inspired consecutive top four finishes in 2009 and 2010, could not. Perth-based smart building materials company ClearVue Technologies has secured a US$500,000 (A$712,450) grant from the United States Department of Energy (DOE) to accelerate its push into the American market. In partnership with North American solar manufacturer Silfab Solar, the company will use the funds to advance its high-efficiency building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) spandrel technology. ClearVue Technologies is developing integrated solar glazing and façades for energy-generating surfaces. Solar external cladding comes in a wide range of colours to complement new and retrofit construction designs. The grant supports a US Department of Energy (DOE) initiative titled “Development of High Efficiency Silicon Solar Spandrels”, which aims to combine ClearVue’s expertise in solar-integrated architectural glazing with Silfab’s significant photovoltaic manufacturing capabilities. The scope covers technical development, performance validation, and evaluation of viable US manufacturing pathways. The DOE-backed project lands as the United States seeks to push solar power generation beyond conventional rooftops and into the fabric of buildings. The department has identified façades, windows, skylights, spandrels and other architectural elements as potential platforms for BIPV, while federal programs have targeted innovation and domestic solar manufacturing.

Advertisement

‘With our Hong Kong operation now established and increasing international opportunities, we’re taking our technology to a global market.’ ClearVue chief executive officer and managing director Doug Hunt This initial US$500,000 phase is designated for testing and demonstration at the advanced Silfab Solar Manufacturing Facility in Burlington, Washington, focusing closely on the structural hurdles of merging module production with commercial glass facade installation. ClearVue’s solar spandrel technology is designed to transform the traditionally passive and opaque sections of a building’s façade into active, energy-generating surfaces, all while maintaining architectural design integrity and thermal performance. In a modern glass curtain wall system, the spandrel zone is the opaque section of the façade located between the head of one window and the sill of the window on the floor above. Spandrel panels can account for a substantial proportion of a modern high-rise building’s external walls, yet traditionally do little more than provide insulation and conceal structural elements. ClearVue’s technology aims to turn that under-utilised real estate into productive, electricity-generating surfaces. While it looks like seamless passive glazing from the street, ClearVue’s solar spandrel system integrates directly into standard framing platforms, actively resolving the intense engineering conflicts of a modern curtain wall - extreme thermal stress, venting, fire compliance and weather sealing - while also generating up to 200 watts per square metre of solar power.

Advertisement

ClearVue says its collaboration with Silfab offers a major opportunity, allowing it to refine its technology for US market requirements, including product integration, performance testing and manufacturing evaluation. ClearVue’s new partnership also dovetails neatly with Silfab’s own expansion of its US manufacturing base. The expansion includes a reported US$150 million (A$214M) investment to establish a flagship solar cell and module manufacturing facility in York County, South Carolina, expected to create up to 800 jobs. ClearVue says a move into US manufacturing could also generate additional licensing revenue from its proprietary junction box and some of its other proprietary technologies, fitting in with the company’s capital-light business model of licensing out its intellectual property to established original equipment manufacturers. ClearVue chief executive officer and managing director Doug Hunt said: “This is another significant milestone for ClearVue and further recognition of our technology on the international stage. Securing support through the US Department of Energy, alongside an established American solar manufacturer, reinforces the growing international recognition of ClearVue’s technology and its potential to transform the way buildings generate energy.” The US government grant is another feather in ClearVue’s cap, following the recent opening of its regional headquarters and showroom in Hong Kong to support growth in Asia.

Advertisement

The company has been building significant commercial momentum, reporting a pipeline of open proposals valued at more than A$60 million as of October last year. It has already secured its first European commercial project in Cyprus and has been confirmed as the successful tenderer for the new Sydney headquarters of global design powerhouse Canva. This latest grant is more than just a handy cash injection. It serves as a powerful endorsement from the US government, placing ClearVue’s technology squarely within a major federal push to bring solar power generation into the very skin of American buildings. With a heavyweight manufacturing partner in Silfab Solar by its side and a potential US production line being explored on Uncle Sam’s dime, this Perth innovator appears to be getting a serious leg-up into one of the world’s largest markets. Smarter planning controls encouraging artificial intelligence companies to develop in special precincts would avoid unwanted US-style data centre clusters in Sydney’s densely populated suburbs, a parliamentary inquiry has found. The committee found that in Sydney, data centre clusters are being built in areas like Lane Cove and Ryde simply because AI companies driven by market forces have found the capacity happens to exist there, not because of effective planning. A NSW parliamentary inquiry has called on the government to consider the cumulative impacts of data centres. James Brickwood The state should instead plan for large-scale data centre development in precincts, supported by shared energy and water infrastructure, rather than as isolated developments, the inquiry found. Lane Cove has become a suburban battleground between AI companies and angry locals, after a cluster of data centres began opening in industrial-zoned parts of the suburb. Community backlash led to data centre proponent Goodman to abandon their $1.2 billion proposal. Now locals in other parts of the state are looking to launch similar campaigns.

Advertisement

Among the 23 recommendations was a request that the government change planning requirements to place a greater emphasis on assessing the cumulative impacts of data centres, and to require AI companies to properly listen and respond to community concerns. The inquiry also found the state government took an “entirely backwards” approach to data centre planning by opening up fast-track processes, including through the Investment Delivery Authority, but didn’t release data centre guidelines until a year later. Related Article Updated

Data centres Project Mars set off a war of words. Now the AI data centre is wiped off the face of earth That authority has endorsed at least 15 data centre projects in NSW valued at $51.89 billion, and the state has more than 60 data centres already operating or under construction. Committee chair and Greens MP Abigail Boyd said fast-track processes like the Investment Delivery Authority, which she dubs the “tech bro concierge service”, are leading to growing anguish in communities concerned about data centres popping up in their backyards.

Advertisement

She pointed to this week’s midterm election results in the US, where anti-data-centre Democrats swept gubernatorial races. “Unless we want to be where America is now, if we want to have actual sensible investment in data centres we need to slow down, pause those approvals and give the community time to breathe,” she said. Data centre projects in Sydney. “If we don’t actually do what we’ve recommended in our report we will end up with people just getting angrier and angrier.” The state government recently removed council powers to automatically trigger a referral to the independent planning commission when they object to a state significant data centre, and increased the number of public objections needed to trigger a referral from 50 to 100.

Advertisement

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has said new data centre projects must pay for their own energy, and must put at least as much energy back into the grid as they take out of it. The NSW inquiry found the rapid growth in electricity demand from data centres has the potential to hinder progress towards emission reduction targets if that growth isn’t matched by a similar growth in energy storage. Related Article Good Weekend AI data centres are springing up in communities across the country. Now, residents are fighting back Data centre proponents will have access to a 75-day express assessment process only if they comply with the state’s new data centre guidelines, which include funding additional water and energy supply. The report stopped short of calling for a pause on new data centre approvals after Labor and Liberal committee members voted together to remove the recommendation from the report. Lane Cove and Penrith councils used their evidence to call for a moratorium on new data centre approvals, citing concerns over community consultations and water and energy consumption. A NSW government spokesperson said many of the committee’s findings reflected what the government already heard while designing the state’s guidelines.

Penny Stephens After having become the red carpet trend of the year, mother-daughter dates are officially having their moment at Flemington. NationalQueenslandDavid Jones collapse What the collapse of David Jones means for Brisbane’s retail landscape Dominique Tassell November 5, 2026 — 4:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
