The collapse of David Jones is expected to deliver a major blow to Brisbane’s retail centres across the city and further compound the sector’s struggles in the ailing Queen Street Mall. David Jones was handed over to administrators and receivers on Thursday, for the first time in its 188 years of trading, after its board voted to appoint voluntary administrators from McGrathNicol. The failed retailer’s lenders appointed FTI Consulting as receivers to the group, who will run the business until it is restructured and put up for sale. Brisbane’s CBD may be left without a department store if the David Jones store at QueensPlaza closes following the chain’s collapse into voluntary administration. Dominique Tassell The store was busier than usual on Thursday afternoon, both with people hoping to use their gift cards while they still could and with staff pulling down displays.

Advertisement

In the shoe section, brands including Steve Madden, Kurt Geiger and Dune had empty displays. A shopper told this masthead they had attempted to buy a pair of shoes but had been told by a staff member they were no longer able to be sold. Empty Steve Madden and Kurt Geiger shoe displays in the David Jones store at QueensPlaza in Brisbane’s CBD. Dominique Tassell Analysis by financial services firm MST Marquee identified all but two stores in Queensland as facing closure. There are four David Jones stores in Brisbane, located in Carindale, Chermside, the CBD and Indooroopilly. There are also two stores on the Gold Coast, at Pacific Fair and Robina, and one store in Sunshine Plaza on the Sunshine Coast.

Advertisement

MST Marquee expected all stores bar Chermside and Pacific Fair would close. However, QUT professor and retail expert Gary Mortimer said he believed the CBD store would remain open. An empty Dune shoe display in the David Jones store at QueensPlaza in Brisbane’s CBD. Dominique Tassell “There’s been no official announcement yet on which stores will close in Queensland,” he said. “QueensPlaza is a premium destination. That would be a store I would imagine would remain.” Mortimer said several stores that had undergone substantial redevelopment, such as Sunshine Plaza and Pacific Fair, would be less likely to close.

Advertisement

“I think there’s a future for this brand,” he said. “It is the oldest department store in the world, older than Harrods, older than Macy’s. There’s a lot of nostalgia and history connected to that brand, particularly here in Queensland.” The older shopping centres may be less attractive, Mortimer said. Previously, Myer stores have been replaced by retailers such as Kmart, Target and TK Maxx that are large but not big enough to fill the entire space. A closure of the David Jones in QueensPlaza would leave the CBD without a department store, after Myer vacated the old Myer Centre – now known as Uptown – in July 2023.

Advertisement

Vicinity Centres owns both QueensPlaza and Uptown, after it completed a takeover of the latter earlier this year. In its ASX announcement, Vicinity said it “maintains contingency plans for each of its David Jones locations and routinely assesses alternative uses for major tenancy space as part of its asset planning”. Experts argue there may be an excess of retail space in Brisbane’s CBD. Catherine Strohfeldt The company said in February the revitalised Uptown would combine fashion, dining, technology, leisure and entertainment stores, and would mirror the Emporium in Melbourne’s CBD. It estimated the redevelopment would cost $300-$350 million – funded through debt and the sale of other assets – and would be completed by 2029.

Advertisement

Advertisement

The proposal would replace the existing Wintergarden shopping centre with a six-storey retail podium topped by a 45-storey hotel, residential tower and a 16-storey office tower. Mortimer said there was an excess of retail space in the CBD, while locals have moved to centres such as Carindale and Chermside for their shopping. The old entrance to Myer from Queen Street Mall is still permanently closed, and the windows covered in hoarding. Marissa Calligeros “We don’t go into the CBD to shop any more, unless it’s for that luxurious experience which you get at QueensPlaza and Edward Street,” he said. “I think Wintergarden is well positioned to leverage that market, so I do think we will see a redeveloped Wintergarden. Potentially with a Myer store. Brisbane is the only capital city in Australia without a flagship Myer store.

Advertisement

“But of course that then creates some challenges for Uptown, which appears to have still not made any investment in that centre.” Rumours have swirled for years about a possible Myer comeback in the CBD, but none have eventuated, so exactly who would occupy all this retail space is up in the air. Empty shelves at the Indooroopilly David Jones. Mortimer said he would like to see Uptown, which has direct access to a bus station and plenty of parking, reinvigorated as a health services centre to accommodate workers and the growing number of people living centrally. David Jones’ collapse was triggered after the department store operator’s private equity owners failed to reach a deal with major landlord Scentre Group on store closures and its rent bill.

Advertisement

Scentre Group, which operates Westfield Carindale and Westfield Chermside, rejected a restructuring proposal put forward by David Jones. A counter-proposal by Scentre was subsequently rejected by David Jones’ board of directors on Wednesday. Related Article Analysis

David Jones collapse The billionaire who’s a winner from David Jones’ collapse Scentre Group chief executive Elliott Rusanow said David Jones had not paid rent since October and “therefore are in breach”. Rusanow said its offer would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading. “That offer has disappointingly been rejected by them,” he said.

Advertisement

In its ASX announcement, Vicinity identified David Jones as having an outstanding rent bill of approximately $2.2 million as of October 31. Children starting school will learn about financial concepts as part of maths lessons to keep the Australian curriculum relevant and help them grasp the foundational skills as international standings in numeracy slide. Education ministers announced the biggest change to the national curriculum in years on Thursday, including streamlining maths content in the first three years of school to ensure what students learn builds on itself. The main focus of foundation to year 2 remains on teaching maths, with the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority now breaking down content into explicit, sequential steps for teachers to follow. St Bernard’s School maths leader Nick Flavel with students Thea Nolan and Zavier Perez, who learn about cash in primary school despite growing up in an increasingly cashless society. Justin McManus But students will also encounter money in their lessons as a way of applying the concepts they learn and preparing them to have greater financial literacy in later years, with studies showing people confident in their numeracy skills often have higher financial and health outcomes.

Advertisement

“We’re not teaching five-year-olds about superannuation,” said ACARA chief executive Stephen Gniel. Related Article Opinion

Money psychology Why working harder won’t make you rich – and what to do instead Paridhi Jain Money contributor “We’re giving them the foundations they need to become financially literate adults. By developing essential mathematical skills such as addition, subtraction, multiplication and fractions, students build the knowledge and confidence they’ll need to understand more complex financial concepts later in life.” However, in an increasingly cashless society, teachers are grappling with how to introduce their youngest students to financial concepts. At St Bernard’s School in Coburg East, maths leader Nick Flavel said lessons still relied on teaching students about cash. “It’s a difficult concept to teach because we are living in a cashless and digital world. They have grown up watching their parents pay for things with a phone,” he said.

Advertisement

“They almost need something tangible there to understand it’s worth something. If it’s just a balance on a spreadsheet, then it almost doesn’t mean anything, but if there’s cash there, then it’s visibly worth something.” Related Article Education Maths enrolments rebound, but one group is taking longer to bounce back Carly Sawatzki, a senior lecturer at Deakin University who researches financial education in schools, said linking maths with financial literacy during early years helped bring real-world application to maths for many students, but only if they learnt about the world they were living in. “Many children don’t see financial exchange taking place with notes and coins,” Sawatzki said. “The challenge for the curriculum writers and then of course school teachers as well is to figure out well what other sorts of examples of financial exchange might be relevant for very young children to be learning about … Children might receive gift cards for cultural celebrations, for example, so that’s a different way they are experiencing money.”

Advertisement

Advertisement

The curriculum will now also ensure early primary school students learn about broad concepts of identity, family and belonging, before later learning about community, diversity and respect. Secondary school students will learn about antisemitism and other forms of hate in classes including history. These changes, which follow recommendations by David Gonski’s antisemitism education taskforce, accompany content about Jewish history, culture and its contributions to Australia more broadly at the request of the Jewish community, who did not want the new content to only focus on educating students about the Holocaust. Education ministers have also tasked the curriculum authority with investigating whether to make civics compulsory for year 9s and 10s nationwide after research showed high school students’ understanding of democracy had dropped to its lowest level since testing began in 2004. “Schools don’t just teach numeracy, literacy and critical thinking skills. Claire Ewart-Kennedy, Strathbogie Shire deputy mayor and a former chief of staff to Josh Frydenberg, confirmed to The Age on Thursday she had lodged a nomination to become a VRC director. title: What David Jones' administration means for shoppers, stores and gift cards
text:
In Brief David Jones has entered voluntary administration after negotiations with Westfield's owner fell apart.

The company will keep trading, but it is believed that at least some of its physical stores will close.

After 188 years, David Jones has entered voluntary administration after crisis meetings between the department store's owners and landlords failed to reach an agreement.

The retailer will continue to trade while administrators review its operations, but some store closures are expected as the future of the business is assessed.

The move follows years of losses and comes amid mounting pressure on traditional department stores from changing shopping habits, online rivals and specialty retailers.

How did David Jones get here?

The high-end chain has been struggling in recent years, like many department stores around the world, in the face of changing consumer behaviour and the rise of ultra-cheap online shopping and specialty retailers such as Mecca.

South Africa-based Woolworths Holdings shelled out $2.1 billion to acquire the then stock exchange-listed group in 2014, before selling it to Sydney-based private equity firm Anchorage Capital for just $100 million in 2023.

Despite efforts to revive the retailer, Anchorage has been unable to turn the business around.

David Jones posted a $95.5 million loss for 2024-25, after a $74 million loss for 2023-24.

The company is yet to file its results for 2025-26 after missing an October deadline.

Why has David Jones entered administration now?

David Jones has not paid rent to Westfield, its biggest landlord, since September. Seventeen of the retailer's remaining 38 stores are in shopping centres owned by Scentre Group.

According to Scentre Group, David Jones paid $45 million in rent for the first nine months of the year, up to 30 September, while landlords also hold $45 million in bank guarantees that could be used to cover rent obligations.

But negotiations between the two parties broke down, with Scentre Group chief executive Elliott Rusanow saying David Jones was in breach of its lease agreements.

"We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital Partners that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading and that offer has disappointingly been rejected by them," Rusanow said.

According to reporting by the Australian Financial Review, the company had been in talks with landlords over plans to close some physical stores.

What happens now?

David Jones will continue to trade under the control of administrators while its operations are reviewed, but it is believed at least some stores will close.

What does it mean for shoppers?

Erin Turner from the Consumer Policy Research Centre said the department store was entering a "period of uncertainty".

"This means that if you've got a gift card, you want to use it as quickly as possible," she told ABC News.

"If in the worst case, the company stops trading and closes its doors, you'll be considered an unsecured creditor and that means that you'll be waiting months or years to see if you get any of that money back."

She said it was possible accrued loyalty points and items on lay-by may not be honoured.

"In past company collapses, the big one is Dick Smith in 2016, we saw that people lost money that they had in gift cards, and even in deposits they'd made on some items that they'd pre-purchased."

While administrators have said David Jones will continue to trade, Turner warned consumers against buying gift cards or making lay-by purchases until there is more certainty about the retailer's future.

Australia is entering the end-of-year sales season, but Gary Mortimer, a retail marketing researcher at Queensland University of Technology, does not expect heavy discounting at David Jones.

"A lot of the David Jones model is the concession model," Mortimer said. "Those brands own that space and own that inventory."

He said many brands would likely remove stock from any shuttered stores and shift it to other locations.

Despite stores remaining open, some people online have speculated this may already be happening, sharing photos on social media they say show concession outlets being packed up.

While David Jones-branded products in closed stores could be discounted, Mortimer said the retailer may instead transfer much of that stock to remaining stores, limiting the scale of any clearance sales.

— With reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

title: The hidden cost of living in Australia's mining heartland
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Along the highways that trace Western Australia's Pilbara coastline, industrial salt pans stretch flat to the horizon, broken only by the railway lines that carry iron ore to the sea.

Beyond them, mounds of rust-coloured boulders rise from the spinifex, stacked as if tipped out by hand.

Here, the dry heat settles in early, before the sun has fully cleared the horizon.

This is mining country, home to some of the most lucrative stretches of land in Australia. Every day, vast shipments laden with hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of natural gas, salt and iron ore leave these shores, making their way into global supply chains.

Yet in this resource-rich environment, one of the most basic necessities is surprisingly hard to come by.

Across the Pilbara, access to fresh food is precarious: truckloads of fruit and vegetables must travel thousands of kilometres to reach remote communities in the region. The distance drives up cost, and supply can be unreliable.

Roebourne, or Ieramugadu as it is known by its Traditional Owners, is one such community.

The glow of Woodside's gas flares on Murujuga, the Burrup Peninsula, seen from the top of Mount Welcome in Roebourne (Ieramugadu). Source: SBS News

Hemmed in by rail lines heavy with iron ore, road trains thundering past and the gas plants of the seaboard, it is the oldest town in the north-west and home to a predominantly Aboriginal community of fewer than 1,000 people on Ngarluma country.

It is here, at the furthest reach of the food supply chain, that fresh produce and pantry staples arrive last, if at all.

Inside Roebourne's fight for fresh food

When SBS News visits in early spring, the shelves of the Ieramugadu store on Roebourne's main strip are unusually abundant. Located on Roe Street, it is the only place in town to buy fresh produce, with the nearest supermarkets 13km away in Wickham and 40km away in Karratha.

In the adjoining café, Amieriya Samson is already at the coffee machine. Affectionately known as Dolly, the softly spoken 21-year-old with a shy smile is one of the most familiar faces in town.

Plastered to the side of the machine is a word that guides the social enterprise she works within: 'nyinyart', meaning reciprocity, sharing and looking after one another.

Dolly Samson tips fine patterns into each cup with a practised ease at odds with her bashfulness, serving elders, locals and the transient miners passing through the café. Source: SBS News

"It's very busy. It's beautiful," the Ngarluma and Nyamal woman tells SBS News, gesturing to the street outside, which, until the café opened, was largely deserted.

"Locals, elders and other people coming in having tea, cakes and just coming in to see us, see their grandchildren working. I feel like it makes them happy."

Samson is proud that people here have watched her "grow up in this community" and then stay to serve in it, a path she says has made her "a young role model" too.

But Roebourne has not always had this hub, and there was a time, only a few years ago, when the shelves around her frequently stood empty.

Almost everything the remote town eats is hauled thousands of kilometres by road train from the state's south-west and other supply centres, through wheat country and saltbush, into the red-dirt Pilbara.

Along the way, regional centres draw on the same supply network, while Roebourne's distance from major distribution hubs adds to the cost and complexity of getting food to its shelves. Perishable goods are particularly vulnerable to delays and handling conditions, and transport costs can affect retail prices.

In October 2019, those costs forced Roebourne's only grocery store to close its doors, leaving residents with scant options for buying food locally.

For the next two years, residents had to rely on the lone service station's dehydrated and long-life stock to fill their pantries. Buying fresh food often meant travelling to Wickham or Karratha — a difficult option in a community with low rates of car ownership and licensing.

Greens became so hard to come by that the local pub raffled bags of salad leaves, a prize usually reserved for the meat tray.

In December 2021, the Ngarluma Yindjibarndi Foundation (NYFL), which represents the Ngarluma Traditional Owners and the neighbouring Yindjibarndi people, reopened the doors with backing from local government and industry.

Bridging the food gap

NYFL sources its stock wherever it can: fruit too blemished for the major chains, goods in mislabelled packaging, surplus from the nearest supermarkets, meals frozen by mine-site caterers and deliveries secured through arrangements with industry partners.

Run as a social enterprise, the reopening of the Ieramugadu store has single-handedly restored Roebourne's access to fresh food. In 2025, it distributed 16.2 tonnes of donated food to the community, according to NYFL data.

Around 1,500km north of Perth, Roebourne was gazetted in 1866 and grew as a hub for the pastoralists and pearlers who pushed into the north-west. Source: Getty / Manfred Gottschalk

Tourists pay the shelf price, while members discreetly use a card at the register to access discounted staples, sometimes at no cost — a dignified transaction designed to be indistinguishable from any other in the queue.

The model combines retail sales, donated food, and member support, helping the store serve customers with varying levels of financial need. But donations and surplus stock can be unpredictable, and the availability of particular products depends on what suppliers can provide.

Locals tell SBS News that irregular deliveries, poor-quality produce, fuel disruptions and floods that cut the roads along the supply chain still leave them regularly going without.

When deliveries fall short, the store turns to what it grows.

Cultivating food in Roebourne presents its own challenges. In 1864, settlers drove sheep onto the plains at the foot of Mount Welcome, where the town now stands. Generations of grazing — first sheep and then cattle — contributed to landscape degradation, leaving ground that some now describe as "dead earth".

With scant rain and fierce summer heat, little grows here without help.

Yet out the back of the store, a lush community garden tumbles from expansive beds built by inmates at the nearby Roebourne Regional Prison.

Beyond the harvest, the garden doubles as a classroom, where young people learn to grow food and live from the land. Source: SBS News

Glossy banana leaves fan over sprawling pumpkin vines and their yellow flowers, while young fruit trees, bush foods and native herbs crowd the beds between them. In 2025, the garden yielded more than 60kg of vegetables for the store.

Samson often comes out here to pick tomatoes for the shelves and flowers for the café.

"We collect [the produce], weigh it and put it in the food section of the store for the community," she says.

Store manager Bec Gregory, who moved to Roebourne from the Kimberley, wants the young staff to see the whole journey, from the garden beds to the kitchen to the Elders it feeds.

"A lot of them then have purpose to come to work because they're providing for their own family, serving their Elders, which is a privilege in itself," she tells SBS News.

Bec Gregory manages the Ieramugadu store and café, where unclaimed food is turned into compost for the garden or cooked into café meals. Source: SBS News

Many start as school students on traineeships, she explains: "So if we start them young, hopefully they'll keep going."

Beyond empty shelves

Empty shelves are only the most visible of Roebourne's shortages.

The town is one of only seven places in Australia to have recorded temperatures above 50C; homes under corrugated iron roofs hold the summer heat like kilns, and families spill onto porches as the power and internet cut out.

Data reveals a stark health burden.

At the 2021 Census, diabetes was reported by 20.9 per cent of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander residents in Roebourne, compared with 5.9 per cent nationally. Kidney disease was reported by 3.2 per cent, compared with 1.2 per cent nationally.

Diabetes, closely tied to diet, was reported by one in five of the town's Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander residents at the 2021 Census. Source: SBS News

Beyond these statistics are lives shaped by illness and loss.

In the NYFL office, a noticeboard is seldom without word of someone who has passed.

Saturdays are set aside for funerals, and sorry business is perpetual — much of the grief, residents say, is for young men, making loss a constant presence in community life.

In one of the store's aisles, we are greeted by Dorothy, who was widowed at 35. She is wearing a T-shirt screen-printed with a photo of her late husband.

READ MORE Australian gas giant and Traditional Owners locked in $300 million compensation battle

Almost all of the available data about the town has been gathered by outside institutions, with limited community control over its collection, interpretation and use.

For Aaralyn Lockyer, a 22-year-old Yindjibarndi woman, that is the problem at the heart of her work as a community researcher on NYFL's Ieramugadu Indigenous Data Sovereignty Project, one of the first community-led data projects of its kind in Western Australia.

"We want to have sovereignty over our data rather than having it in organisations outside of Roebourne," she tells SBS News.

We wanted to have it housed inside of NYFL and be community-controlled rather than elsewhere.

The project's first analysis, drawing on Census and socio-economic data, found Roebourne ranks among the most disadvantaged places in the country, with an estimated 87 per cent of Indigenous residents earning less than $805 a week, the national median personal weekly income recorded at the 2021 Census.

But Lockyer says many find the Census itself "quite intimidating", its official form a barrier for anyone not "well versed in reading and writing".

Working with the Australian National University, the project is now building its own measures of wellbeing. These include questions about whether people feel strong in their culture and can speak their language — tested through community focus groups.

The goal, NYFL says, is for the services, policy and investment that reach Roebourne to be shaped by what its people say they need.

A national food security problem

Roebourne sits on the frontline of affordability pressures now being felt across the country.

Foodbank's 2026 Hunger Report found one in three Australian households, or 3.6 million homes, experienced food insecurity in the past year, with the rate among First Nations households reaching 57 per cent.

The report describes people in regional areas "choosing fuel over food".

Nearly half of food-insecure households told Foodbank’s 2026 Hunger Report that embarrassment had kept them from seeking help. Source: SBS News

Elizabeth Jackson, an associate professor of supply chain management and logistics at Curtin University, says fuel accounts for "the lion's share" of the cost of moving food, and the risk does not end when the truck is unloaded.

"The freshness and perishability of many of the products that are being transported are very vulnerable. It's not only that [food is] vulnerable on its journey, but it's vulnerable when it gets to the destination as well," she tells SBS News.

"The more remote the community, the less access it has to reliable power sources, for example.

It's a basic human right to have access to safe and nutritious food.

Desert communities around Newman, in the inland Pilbara, are interested in adopting the store's social enterprise model. But Roebourne has a logistical advantage that may be difficult to replicate elsewhere: proximity to the North West Coastal Highway, the region's main arterial route, where freight already travels.

Even so, a store built on nyinyart can only stock what reaches it.

For Ngarluma custodian Sam Walker, the problem extends beyond supermarket shelves to the loss of access to traditional food sources. She says mining and the infrastructure surrounding it have restricted her community's ability to hunt and gather on country.

For all its hardship, Sam Walker calls life in Roebourne "a blessing", in a community where "we share everything … just to survive". Source: SBS News

"My people, all Indigenous people that are affected by mining, can never ever have the same diet as their ancestors, or the ones that are still living in their homelands that mining hasn't reached yet," she tells SBS News, speaking of the bush that once fed her people, much of it now cleaved by fences and mining tenements.

That's not available to my people anymore, and it hasn't been for a very long time.

For now, Roebourne is tenuously sustained by what the road trains bring and what it can grow itself.

And on the small patch of country it can still firmly call its own, the garden hangs heavy with fruit, a reminder that in its people's hands, this land has never stopped giving.

This article is the first in a special two-part series on food insecurity in Indigenous communities.

title: 'Still a lot of optimism': The surprising finding in a survey of 10,000 Australians
text:
In brief Economic and housing pressures are leading to a growing sense of pessimism in Australia.

But communities appear to be remaining strong, with an expert saying adversity can help create social cohesion.

Australians are increasingly despairing about the country's future, with cost of living pressures, housing affordability and global conflicts weighing on public confidence.

But despite growing concerns about the country's direction, a new national survey has found Australians still feel a strong sense of belonging in their local communities, helping keep social cohesion steady.

Researchers behind the Scanlon Social Cohesion report, released on Thursday, surveyed 10,000 Australians from diverse backgrounds and political leanings to gauge national values and attitudes.

Topics ranged from the cost of living and immigration to acceptance of different faiths and backgrounds, combining to create an index score of 78, consistent with the last three years.

"In some way there is a strong sense of pessimism among many Australians," the Scanlon Foundation Research Institute's head Anthea Hancocks told SBS News.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"But there is still a lot of optimism as well. People feel like they can rely on their neighbours and find support locally. That’s important in keeping social cohesion."

Cost of living is making Australians worried for the future

Of those surveyed, just under half said cost of living, inflation or housing was the most important issue facing Australia today.

Hancocks said these pressures are placing an "increasing strain on Australia’s social cohesion" and exacerbating people's fears.

Almost half of adults are pessimistic or very pessimistic about Australia’s future, up from 43 per cent in 2025 and 31 per cent in 2018.

And one in three adults believed their life will be a little or a lot worse in the next three or four years, up from 29 per cent last year.

Source: SBS News

Dr James O'Donnell, a senior lecturer from the School of Demography at the Australian National University, authored the report and went into greater detail on the results.

"At least one in five of us are saying we're sometimes going without health or medical care, and 10 per cent of us are saying that we're poor or struggling or we're missing out on meals or not being able to pay the rent or mortgage," he said.

Attitudes towards different faiths are shifting

The report also examines perceptions of people of different faiths.

O'Donnell said that in the past few years, new patterns have emerged that could be linked to global conflicts and the politicisation of different religions and cultural backgrounds.

READ MORE The growing divides shaping Australians' trust in democracy

A stark example is people's attitudes towards Muslims, which had been improving until 2023, the year the conflict between Hamas and Israel boiled over.

In 2026, 43 per cent of respondents had negative attitudes towards Muslims, with 18 per cent being very negative.

There's been a similar trend towards Jewish people, where the proportion now that have a negative attitude overall towards the group is up to 18 per cent from 13 per cent in 2024.

Source: SBS News

There has also been declining attitudes towards Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists and greater support for Christians reported.

"Current conflicts in Gaza and elsewhere are seeing pressures on our intercultural harmony and connection," O'Donnell said.

"That’s also feeding off support generally dropping for diversity and more negative attitudes towards immigrants coming from various parts of Asia and Africa."

Australians have become more divided in their views on immigration

In 2026, 59 per cent of respondents said the level of immigration to Australia is too high, up from 52 per cent in 2025 and significantly higher than an average of 39 per cent in the 2010s.

Concerns about the scale of immigration were driven by One Nation and Coalition supporters, while Greens and Labor voters' views remained unchanged from last year.

Source: SBS News

Net overseas migration (NOM), the number of arrivals into Australia less departures, reached a peak of nearly 550,000 to 556,000 during 2022–2023.

Recent NOM figures have fallen to roughly 301,000–340,800 for 2024-2025, with the government pledging a target of 225,000 by 2028.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

While more Australians believe immigration levels are too high, support for multiculturalism remains strong, suggesting concerns about the scale of migration do not necessarily translate into opposition to Australia's multicultural identity.

Over three-quarters of those surveyed believe immigrants are just as likely to be good citizens as Australians born here and agree that multiculturalism has benefited the country.

Despite pressures, people feel they belong and like their neighbours

A look at over 20 years of the annual Scanlon surveys shows cohesion has declined over the longer term but has not deteriorated further in recent years.

This could be largely attributed to positive attitudes towards our local communities and neighbours.

Hancocks said that while many respondents expressed disappointment with the kind of society we are currently living in, the "hallmarks of what make a society strong remain".

Australians overwhelmingly feel they belong in their neighbourhoods, and 81 per cent agree people are willing to help their neighbours.

Source: SBS News

People from different national or ethnic backgrounds get on well with others, according to 79 per cent of respondents, and 64 per cent said their neighbourhood has a sense of community.

Adversity can lead to cohesion

Dr Michael Noetel, a clinical psychologist and senior lecturer at the University of Queensland, told SBS News that our environments have large and varied effects on our behaviour and attitudes.

While it is impossible to predict how events impact every person's perception of an issue or group, there are patterns.

"When you are comfortable, and your needs are met, then you are better able to prioritise less critical things in your life," he explained.

"But when that security is threatened, then you really just have to look after your own family and your neighbours."

He pointed to the COVID-19 pandemic, saying that some communities became more tightly knit, leading to a sense of "solidarity in the face of that adversity".

title: A GLP-1 weight loss pill has been approved in Australia. Here's what we know
text:
IN BRIEF The Therapeutic Goods Administration has approved the use of the Wegovy tablet in Australia.

The eligibility for Australians accessing subsidised GLP-1 medication remains limited.

Australians wanting to take weight-loss drugs will no longer have to inject themselves, with the first daily tablet version now medically approved.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) cleared various doses of the Wegovy tablet, made by Danish pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, on Tuesday.

Previously, Australians had to take the GLP-1 weight-loss drug in the form of a weekly injection.

The daily tablet form of the appetite-suppressing medication was approved for use in the UK in June and in the US late last year.

Novo Nordisk said it expected the pill would be available in Australia before the end of the year.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We will share confirmed availability timing as soon as we can," a spokesperson said.

Endocrinologist John Wentworth welcomed the news, saying it would make the drug easier for patients to take.

He said trial data indicated the tablet version of the drug worked just as well as the jabs.

He told ABC News Breakfast that many individuals prefer to avoid self-injecting, particularly when travelling.

"People don't like injecting themselves ... they're going on a holiday," he said.

"So instead of taking the needles, they'll transition onto the tablets and then come back."

How much will the medication cost, and will it be subsidised?

The TGA said it had approved the drug for weight management and for reducing the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, like stroke or heart attack, in eligible adults.

The tablets have been approved in 1.5mg, 4mg, 9mg and 25mg strengths, and added to the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods.

The price of the pill version of the drugs has not been announced, but the injectables are not on Australia's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, except for those with Type 2 Diabetes.

As a result, about 400,000 Australians currently pay up to $5,000 a year to access Wegovy, Ozempic and other GLP-1 weight-loss drugs.

The federal government is currently in negotiations with the manufacturer to bring Wegovy onto the scheme for a small cohort of extra patients, which would bring the price down to $25 per script or $7.70 for concession card holders.

The approval would also make the drug cheaper and more accessible, Wentworth said.

"When the price comes down, we will be treating these just as we treat a blood pressure or a cholesterol medication because they have such powerful benefits to keep us well for longer."

A Department of Health spokesperson told SBS News that a medicine must be assessed and recommended by the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee (PBAC) before it can be subsidised through the PBS for a particular condition.

"The PBAC assesses evidence about how well a medicine works and how safe it is compared to therapies already funded in Australia, as well as value for money.

"Pharmaceutical companies are responsible for making submissions seeking PBS subsidy, and the government cannot compel a company to make a submission or pre-empt the independent advice of the PBAC."

title: 'A shameful chapter of history': King Charles withholds apology for slavery in the Caribbean
text:
Key Points The Commonwealth summit gathered 56 members states to Antigua to meet with the King.

Buckingham Palace has repeatedly ruled out financial reparations over its role in the transatlantic slave trade.

King Charles has told Commonwealth leaders the transatlantic slave trade "fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow", but did not offer an apology.

In his address to presidents and prime ministers at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua, Charles said his commitment was growing to find ways to "address the wrongs of the past with action for the future".

The ‌run-up to the gathering of the 56 member states, which comprise mostly former British colonies, has been dominated by talk of whether Britain should apologise or pay reparations for the role it played in the transatlantic slave trade.

He delivered his speech on Tuesday against the background of UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announcing a change in long-established government policy and making an offer of talks on a slavery apology but not financial reparations.

"Our history inspires us, can appal us, yet it can always teach us. We cannot change the actions of those who came before us. We can, however, learn from the past," he said.

"The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth ... that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.

"And yet history also teaches us that evil need not have the last word; that character and courage can combine to overcome the most monstrous injustice, as they did with the determination to end international trade in enslaved people, in which the Royal Navy played such a leading role.

"The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."

Charles also told the gathering of world leaders: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know."

"Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures — the good they did as well as the wrongs."

Calls for an apology and reparations from the UK have been growing in recent years and St Lucia's Prime Minister Philip J Pierre, chairman of the 15-member Caribbean Community, has reportedly said the economic and political bloc was "ready to engage" in the structured dialogue Burnham offered.

Burnham has also gone further than his predecessors by saying he was open to Britain apologising for slavery and officials were holding talks with national ‌leaders at the summit to discuss what form that could take.

Major ticket merchants are accused of twisting the knife in Australians already battling a cost of living crisis.

On Wednesday, Consumer advocacy group Choice revealed its annual Shonky Award winners, calling out the products and services it deems the most dodgy.

Ticketek and Ticketmaster featured on the list for what the group labelled as gouging customers with sneaky tactics.

Both merchants allow dynamic pricing schemes, through which ticket costs can rise during sale periods.

title: The Australian territory where online forms, banks and services don't always work
text:
Norfolk Island is, legally speaking, part of Australia. But running a business in this remote Pacific territory, home to around 2,100 residents, can be very different from on the mainland.

Government forms can reject local telephone numbers and banking services can be difficult to access. Even routine changes to internet services can leave businesses disconnected.

This speaks to its geographic challenges — Norfolk lies some 1,500km from the Australian mainland — as well as some unique complexities stemming from its unusual political and administrative history.

In 1856, following the closure of its British penal settlements, Norfolk became home to descendants of the HMS Bounty mutineers and Tahitians from Pitcairn Island. The Pitcairn community brought its own traditions and governing practices, which helped shape Norfolk’s distinctive identity long before it became an Australian territory in 1914.

Norfolk gained a substantial degree of self-government in 1979, before Canberra abolished the arrangement in 2015. Australian taxation, employment laws, Medicare and social security followed, bringing benefits alongside new obligations. The island’s regional council has been under administration since 2021, while disputes over its governance continue.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Now, a new survey of Norfolk Island businesses examines the difficulties they face, from freight and insurance costs to navigating laws and commercial systems designed for mainland Australia.

An unusual economy, under pressure

The Business Council of Norfolk Island received responses from 103 of 239 businesses contacted, with nearly half reporting worsening conditions over the past year. Long-established businesses were particularly affected, with 27 of 42 reporting deterioration, compared with four of 21 established in the past three years.

Freight was the biggest concern, identified by 70 per cent of respondents who answered the question, followed by insurance at 45 per cent. Other concerns included visitor spending, telecommunications and air services.

Norfolk has no conventional deep-water port. Cargo ships anchor offshore while cranes lower goods into smaller vessels, known as lighters. These shuttle to the pier, where freight is lifted ashore. Heavy seas can interrupt unloading, while biosecurity requirements complicate imports.

READ MORE Why one tiny island's Census is about much more than numbers

New Commonwealth-funded cargo-transfer vessels have been introduced, but freight still requires specialised handling. Changes to shipping connections with New Zealand have complicated supply arrangements, while air freight provides a more frequent but expensive alternative.

Businesses must plan orders around shipping schedules, allow for delays and find alternative supplies when deliveries are disrupted. While some costs are unavoidable, managing these disruptions takes considerable time and effort. Other difficulties arise from government and commercial systems that don’t accommodate the island’s circumstances.

Norfolk’s five-digit telephone numbers don’t always fit online forms designed for mainland Australia. A 2023 parliamentary inquiry heard of online forms rejecting local numbers, including during Australian Business Number applications.

Norfolk Island is home to around 2,100 residents. Source: Getty / Oliver Strewe

Two-factor authentication creates further problems when banking and software services cannot send verification codes to local numbers. Some businesses maintain separate Australian mobile services simply to access everyday services.

Even the island’s postcode, 2899, is assigned to New South Wales by Australia Post, although Norfolk is legally an external territory, creating confusion in commercial systems.

Last month, local users reported Starlink services being suspended following an apparent change in how the company recognised service locations, disrupting businesses reliant on satellite internet.

The incident illustrates how a seemingly minor change in a global provider’s systems can have significant consequences for an isolated community, leaving local businesses to resolve problems they had no part in creating.

The burden of changing rules

Norfolk’s older businesses developed their practices and commercial relationships under different taxation, employment and administrative arrangements. Newer enterprises have operated within the post-2016 system from the outset.

Established businesses may therefore face additional costs adapting longstanding arrangements to newer requirements. This could help explain why older businesses reported worsening conditions more often, although sector, size and market conditions may also play a part.

Norfolk’s legal arrangements add another complication. Businesses operate under a mixture of Commonwealth law, selected state legislation and laws retained from the former Norfolk government. Determining which requirements apply can require specialist advice that’s difficult to obtain locally.

The latest survey found a similar divide between employers and sole operators. Among respondents, 41 per cent of businesses with employees reported adverse effects from laws, regulations or policies, compared with 7 per cent of sole operators.

Norfolk Island is located around 1,500km off the coast of Australia.

Employers must manage payroll, workplace conditions, safety and reporting obligations. These provide important protections, but compliance requires time, resources and expertise that can be difficult to access on the island.

My current research examines how Norfolk Island businesses have adapted to the governance changes introduced a decade ago.

Businesses must plan around uncertain freight deliveries, navigate overlapping legal requirements and find ways to use digital systems that don’t always recognise where they operate. These efforts keep businesses running, but take time and money away from serving customers, improving services and growing their operations.

Norfolk Island illustrates a problem facing other small and remote communities. National and global systems can work efficiently for millions of people while leaving those outside their assumptions to resolve the exceptions themselves.

For Norfolk’s businesses, the difficulty is not simply operating far from the mainland, but the additional time and resources needed to make those systems work.

Rod McNaughton is a professor of entrepreneurship at the University of Auckland, Waipapa Taumata Rau. He received funding for this research from Juncture: Dialogues on Inclusive Capitalism, a research centre within the University of Auckland Business School.

title: See the full list: The jobs Australian employers are struggling most to fill
text:
In Brief New data shows workforce shortages continue to persist in a variety of industries.

Nearly 280 occupations are in shortage across the country, representing 27 per cent of those assessed.

Want to get into horse breeding? Are you a pyschotherapist or a landscape designer? These are just three occupations newly listed as in shortage this year by a government agency.

Other occupations, such as roof tiler, gas fitter, mining engineer, psychologist and podiatrist, have consistently been listed as in shortage each year since 2021.

They are just some of the 127 occupations that have consistently faced worker shortages since 2021. They broadly fall into the field of technicians and trade workers and professionals.

Data from Jobs and Skills Australia shows despite shortages continuing to ease across several fields, companies are still struggling to fill many roles across a variety of industries. Twenty-eight new occupations were in shortage this year, spread across health, science, trades and operations. Some, such as student services adviser and exercise physiologist, are only listed as being in shortage in regional areas.

While technicians and trade workers make up the largest proportion of persistent shortages, other impacted roles tend to be in construction, early childhood education, engineering, health, and science.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The government body suggests three key factors are contributing to shortages: constraints on the supply of potential workers, a lack of suitable applicants and retention issues.

Occupations in shortage tend to have longer vacancy durations and lower rates of being filled.

In industries experiencing a shortage, recruiters tended to identify half as many qualified and suitable candidates. On average, a job offered in an occupation with a shortage received six qualified applicants, and three suitable ones, compared to roles in non-shortage fields which had 13 qualified candidates and six suitable people for the position.

Which occupations are in shortage?

In this year's report, 279 occupations are in shortage across the country, representing 27 per cent of those assessed. The government body says this is down from the peak in 2023, when 36 per cent of assessed roles were in shortage.

Here are the occupations impacted.

How do shortages get addressed?

Professor Larissa Bamberry, a professor of employment and gender relations at the Charles Sturt University School of Business, said discussions around workforce issues tend to use familiar narratives such as "we can't get people, we can't keep people, there aren't enough skilled workers".

"All those things can be true, but one of the most important things I've learnt from working with regional employers and communities is that workforce problems are rarely one single problem," she told SBS News.

"It's usually a mixture of a number of factors tangled together, and they need quite different policy responses."

READ MORE Not just call centres: The skilled Australian jobs now moving offshore

Bamberry said it's better to consider a skills ecosystem approach to assess needs on a region-by-region basis, supported by collaboration between employers, TAFEs and universities to address concerns within that sector and region.

"We tend to go for pipeline responses, which are very much like, 'oh, we will just churn out the right number of people, and we'll hope that those people end up in the right industries and in the right locations'," she said.

"And they often don't."

Regional challenges

Employers in regional areas tend to find it harder to fill vacant roles. In regional areas, 15 occupations are in shortage, decreasing from 21 last year.

Bamberry said a tailored approach allowed policy responses to better address the needs of potential applicants.

Potential issues range from access to public transport, roads, transportation and internet service, through to the distance to education facilities or the demographics of the community.

Instead, she proposes tailoring "the people that we train, the places where we train them, and the industries that we train for".

READ MORE The growing issue that could make migrating to Australia less attractive

In some areas, there may be enough interested workers, but the skills needed for their roles continue to change.

"There's a lot of people who have the knowledge they need for farming, but don't necessarily have the data analysis, sort of technical skills that are required in modern farming these days because we've got AI and we've got so much technological change happening so rapidly," Bamberry said.

The way to fill these roles may be to connect people to the upskilling they seek, rather than increasing the number of potential workers more generally.

"You wouldn't necessarily want to start an international migration program, for example, around horse breeding, but you might have somebody who's got an interest in horse breeding who is in the particular location but hasn't got the particular skills that they need."

title: 'Heartbroken': Spanish footballer dies after collision during match
text:
In brief Jesús de Miguel was hospitalised after an incident during a Spanish second-division match on Monday.

His club, CD Tenerife, announced his "tragic passing" on Tuesday.

A 30-year-old footballer has died a day after colliding with an opponent during a Spanish second-division match, his club said on Tuesday.

Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel died after suffering a cardiac arrest following a collision during a match, CD Tenerife said.

"Racked with pain, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe that this is true, from CD Tenerife we communicate the tragic passing of Jesús de Miguel Alameda," the club said.

"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this feeling overflowing with sadness."

De Miguel was challenging for the ball during a home game on Monday when he was struck in the chest by Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during the final minutes at Estadio Heliodoro Rodríguez López.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

De Miguel was taken to a hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was suspended in the 108th minute.

He lay motionless as players from both teams desperately signalled for medical assistance. Owono was shown a straight red card.

Medical staff treated the player on the pitch for more than five minutes before he was taken to hospital by ambulance.

Tenerife said in a statement that De Miguel died at 8am (local time) on Tuesday. The club, located on Spain's Canary Islands, said it was "heartbroken".

De Miguel, a Madrid native, made his professional debut in 2015 with Leganés B and has since played for a number of lower-divisions clubs in Spain. He joined Tenerife last year.

Tributes flow in

Football clubs across Spain, including Barcelona and Real Madrid, have led tributes following the news of the death.

"Our thoughts and support are with his family, friends and loved ones during these difficult times," Barcelona said in a statement.

Real Madrid also expressed their condolences, stating: "Real Madrid wishes to express its condolences and affection to his family, his teammates, his club, and all his loved ones."

Andorra, which is owned by former Barcelona star Gerard Pique, also offered its condolences.

"We wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel, to all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife. May he rest in peace," Andorra said in a statement.

The Spanish football federation postponed two Copa del Rey matches and one Copa de la Reina match to be held later on Tuesday.

Life-threatening injuries from collisions in football are extremely rare.

Last year in Spain, a 19-year-old goalkeeper died from head injuries suffered during a collision in a fifth-division match. Colindres goalkeeper Raúl Ramírez had two cardiorespiratory arrests, one on the field and then in the ambulance while being transported to a hospital. He was declared brain dead two days later.

In 2001, Ukrainian goalkeeper Serhiy Perkhun was playing for CSKA Moscow when he died from head injuries received in a collision during a match.

Kuniko has maintained a perfect strike rate at its Commonwealth-Silica Hill project 100 kilometres north of Orange in central New South Wales, with all 11 diamond holes from a two-phase, 2731-metre drilling program successfully intersecting gold-silver mineralisation. The company’s latest five-hole, 1492-metre campaign was designed to follow up a spectacular discovery made during phase one drilling and appears to have successfully extended the mineralised system, with step-out holes stretching the known mineralisation by 60m down-dip and 40m up-dip, demonstrating a mineralised extent of roughly 100m. The results are expected to feed into an updated mineral resource estimate slated for December this year. Kuniko’s Commonwealth-Silica Hill project in NSW’s prolific Lachlan Fold Belt. The highlight from the new batch of assays was a 16.3-metre hit grading 1.56 grams per tonne (g/t) gold equivalent from a downhole depth of 75.7m, featuring a higher-grade core of 11.95m at 1.95g/t gold equivalent. This hosted two richer veins of 1.1m assaying 5.17g/t gold equivalent and a 0.65-metre section grading a notable 6.23g/t gold equivalent. Other phase-two results included a broad 43-metre intersection grading 0.31g/t gold equivalent, alongside two 30-metre hits running at 0.45g/t and 0.36g/t gold equivalent, respectively. The company’s primary deposits at Commonwealth and Silica Hill have JORC-inferred mineral resource estimates totalling 88,000 ounces of gold and 3.3 million ounces of silver.

‘These results highlight the broader potential of the Commonwealth-Silica Hill system and will inform the updated mineral resource estimate.’ Kuniko Limited managing director Maja McGuire The latest results appear to complement Kuniko’s initial phase one campaign, which delivered a stunning result when a hole, punched 100 metres beyond the previously defined mineralised footprint, intersected a broad 84-metre zone grading 0.6g/t gold and 123g/t silver. The intercept also contained a 0.5-metre massive sulphide vein grading an eye-watering 27g/t gold and a coffee-spitting 20,603g/t silver, a figure that puts it firmly in bonanza territory, where grades above 1000g/t silver are considered exceptional. Kuniko managing director Maja McGuire said: “The completion of our two diamond drilling campaigns at Commonwealth-Silica Hill represents an important milestone for Kuniko, with all 11 holes intersecting mineralisation and providing substantial new geological and assay information to support our upcoming MRE update later this year. Importantly, we continue to identify opportunities beyond the areas tested by drilling.” The company’s ground sits in the heart of New South Wales’ Lachlan Fold Belt, a tier-one mining jurisdiction often referred to as “elephant country” and host to some of Australia’s largest mineral deposits. The region is seeing a fresh wave of investment as soaring copper prices and a renewed appetite for gold bring the mineral-rich province back into the spotlight. Major operations in the neighbourhood include Newmont’s colossal 39-million-ounce Cadia-Ridgeway mine and Evolution Mining’s Cowal operation. The geology adds another intriguing dimension, with two distinct styles of mineralisation sitting just 200 metres apart: a polymetallic volcanogenic massive sulphide system at the company’s Commonwealth deposit and an epithermal stockwork vein system at Silica Hill. The combination has drawn comparisons with world-class deposits such as Canada’s Eskay Creek, renowned for its exceptionally high-grade precious-metal mineralisation.

Advertisement

With the drills now silent, geophysical interpretation is lighting up the path forward. The company recently deployed downhole electromagnetic (DHEM) probes to hunt for deep, off-hole extensions of conductive sulphides. Integrated gravity, induced polarisation and DHEM surveys have now defined a prospective geophysical trend that stretches for more than 500m to the southeast of the known mineralisation at Silica Hill. The company says significant and untested induced polarisation chargeability anomalies and prospective gravity-low margins have provided a grab bag of additional targets for follow-up exploration. Kuniko appears to be building a district-scale play, with plans advancing for a third phase of drilling in the first quarter of 2027 to test near-resource targets at its Welcome Jack, Walls and Stringers prospects, all set within a kilometre of the existing project resource. Historical drilling at these prospects has already shown promise. A previous hole at Welcome Jack returned 2m at 5.7g/t gold, while drilling at Walls produced a 20-metre intercept grading 0.5g/t gold and 27g/t silver. While its current focus is on the gold-silver potential in NSW, Kuniko also holds a portfolio of battery and critical minerals projects in Norway. These include the Ertelien nickel-copper-cobalt project, which holds a 40-million-tonne resource running 0.25 per cent nickel equivalent, in addition to other cobalt and copper assets aimed at servicing the European energy transition.

With mineralisation hit in every hole to date, Kuniko may have demonstrated it could be onto a significant gold-silver system at Commonwealth-Silica Hill. A resource update is just around the corner and a suite of compelling geophysical and regional targets are lining up for the drill bit. The immediate catalysts are now threefold: final assays, integration of the downhole geophysics and the expected resource update, all of which could help reveal just how big this Lachlan Fold Belt system might be. Gold Coast Titans legend Preston Campbell says any attempts to lure Harry Grant to the Glitter Strip would be on the condition the Kangaroos superstar would be joining for the betterment of the club, rather than simply a lucrative lifestyle change. Grant’s decision not to activate a 2028 player option in his contract with the Melbourne Storm has made the NRL’s leading hooker a free agent. That has since linked the Queensland Maroons dummy-half to the Titans. “There are probably 17 clubs who are going ‘is it worth having a chat to Harry?’ I’d probably put us in the same boat: contemplating,” Titans chief executive Steve Mitchell said. Harry Grant in action against the Kiwis. But Campbell was adamant money could not dictate his signing, and recruitment must not be at the expense of internal player development. There have been some reports which have hinted Grant could seek a lifestyle change, given his love of surfing, which would put the Gold Coast in prime position to make a compelling play. Speaking as the Titans unveiled their 2027 jersey to celebrate the side’s 20th year in the NRL, Campbell told this masthead that as much of a standout talent as Grant was, a move needed to be driven by his desires on the field. Alluding to the form of late-blooming rookie Oliver Pascoe, the club’s founding fullback said a vision to deliver premiership glory to the region must be the priority motivator should Grant arrive.

“To understand why he wants to come here – if he wants to come here – is really important because you’ve got players here right now who want to be here,” Campbell said. “They’ll work really hard and put their body on the line for the club. To have him here is great, but I’ve played at clubs and seen other clubs take on players who have no interest in coming to benefit the club, they come for the lifestyle and the money. “That’s being honest and that’s being real, and you want players at the club who … want to succeed and grow as a player and person, but want to see the club succeed as well.”

Perth-based smart building materials company ClearVue Technologies has secured a US$500,000 (A$712,450) grant from the United States Department of Energy (DOE) to accelerate its push into the American market. In partnership with North American solar manufacturer Silfab Solar, the company will use the funds to advance its high-efficiency building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) spandrel technology. ClearVue Technologies is developing integrated solar glazing and façades for energy-generating surfaces. Solar external cladding comes in a wide range of colours to complement new and retrofit construction designs. The grant supports a US Department of Energy (DOE) initiative titled “Development of High Efficiency Silicon Solar Spandrels”, which aims to combine ClearVue’s expertise in solar-integrated architectural glazing with Silfab’s significant photovoltaic manufacturing capabilities. The scope covers technical development, performance validation, and evaluation of viable US manufacturing pathways. The DOE-backed project lands as the United States seeks to push solar power generation beyond conventional rooftops and into the fabric of buildings. The department has identified façades, windows, skylights, spandrels and other architectural elements as potential platforms for BIPV, while federal programs have targeted innovation and domestic solar manufacturing.

Advertisement

‘With our Hong Kong operation now established and increasing international opportunities, we’re taking our technology to a global market.’ ClearVue chief executive officer and managing director Doug Hunt This initial US$500,000 phase is designated for testing and demonstration at the advanced Silfab Solar Manufacturing Facility in Burlington, Washington, focusing closely on the structural hurdles of merging module production with commercial glass facade installation. ClearVue’s solar spandrel technology is designed to transform the traditionally passive and opaque sections of a building’s façade into active, energy-generating surfaces, all while maintaining architectural design integrity and thermal performance. In a modern glass curtain wall system, the spandrel zone is the opaque section of the façade located between the head of one window and the sill of the window on the floor above. Spandrel panels can account for a substantial proportion of a modern high-rise building’s external walls, yet traditionally do little more than provide insulation and conceal structural elements. ClearVue’s technology aims to turn that under-utilised real estate into productive, electricity-generating surfaces. While it looks like seamless passive glazing from the street, ClearVue’s solar spandrel system integrates directly into standard framing platforms, actively resolving the intense engineering conflicts of a modern curtain wall - extreme thermal stress, venting, fire compliance and weather sealing - while also generating up to 200 watts per square metre of solar power.

Advertisement

ClearVue says its collaboration with Silfab offers a major opportunity, allowing it to refine its technology for US market requirements, including product integration, performance testing and manufacturing evaluation. ClearVue’s new partnership also dovetails neatly with Silfab’s own expansion of its US manufacturing base. The expansion includes a reported US$150 million (A$214M) investment to establish a flagship solar cell and module manufacturing facility in York County, South Carolina, expected to create up to 800 jobs. ClearVue says a move into US manufacturing could also generate additional licensing revenue from its proprietary junction box and some of its other proprietary technologies, fitting in with the company’s capital-light business model of licensing out its intellectual property to established original equipment manufacturers. ClearVue chief executive officer and managing director Doug Hunt said: “This is another significant milestone for ClearVue and further recognition of our technology on the international stage. Securing support through the US Department of Energy, alongside an established American solar manufacturer, reinforces the growing international recognition of ClearVue’s technology and its potential to transform the way buildings generate energy.” The US government grant is another feather in ClearVue’s cap, following the recent opening of its regional headquarters and showroom in Hong Kong to support growth in Asia.

Advertisement

The company has been building significant commercial momentum, reporting a pipeline of open proposals valued at more than A$60 million as of October last year. It has already secured its first European commercial project in Cyprus and has been confirmed as the successful tenderer for the new Sydney headquarters of global design powerhouse Canva. This latest grant is more than just a handy cash injection. It serves as a powerful endorsement from the US government, placing ClearVue’s technology squarely within a major federal push to bring solar power generation into the very skin of American buildings. With a heavyweight manufacturing partner in Silfab Solar by its side and a potential US production line being explored on Uncle Sam’s dime, this Perth innovator appears to be getting a serious leg-up into one of the world’s largest markets. Smarter planning controls encouraging artificial intelligence companies to develop in special precincts would avoid unwanted US-style data centre clusters in Sydney’s densely populated suburbs, a parliamentary inquiry has found. The committee found that in Sydney, data centre clusters are being built in areas like Lane Cove and Ryde simply because AI companies driven by market forces have found the capacity happens to exist there, not because of effective planning. A NSW parliamentary inquiry has called on the government to consider the cumulative impacts of data centres. James Brickwood The state should instead plan for large-scale data centre development in precincts, supported by shared energy and water infrastructure, rather than as isolated developments, the inquiry found. Lane Cove has become a suburban battleground between AI companies and angry locals, after a cluster of data centres began opening in industrial-zoned parts of the suburb. Community backlash led to data centre proponent Goodman to abandon their $1.2 billion proposal. Now locals in other parts of the state are looking to launch similar campaigns.

Advertisement

Among the 23 recommendations was a request that the government change planning requirements to place a greater emphasis on assessing the cumulative impacts of data centres, and to require AI companies to properly listen and respond to community concerns. The inquiry also found the state government took an “entirely backwards” approach to data centre planning by opening up fast-track processes, including through the Investment Delivery Authority, but didn’t release data centre guidelines until a year later. Related Article Updated

Data centres Project Mars set off a war of words. Now the AI data centre is wiped off the face of earth That authority has endorsed at least 15 data centre projects in NSW valued at $51.89 billion, and the state has more than 60 data centres already operating or under construction. Committee chair and Greens MP Abigail Boyd said fast-track processes like the Investment Delivery Authority, which she dubs the “tech bro concierge service”, are leading to growing anguish in communities concerned about data centres popping up in their backyards.

Advertisement

She pointed to this week’s midterm election results in the US, where anti-data-centre Democrats swept gubernatorial races. “Unless we want to be where America is now, if we want to have actual sensible investment in data centres we need to slow down, pause those approvals and give the community time to breathe,” she said. Data centre projects in Sydney. “If we don’t actually do what we’ve recommended in our report we will end up with people just getting angrier and angrier.” The state government recently removed council powers to automatically trigger a referral to the independent planning commission when they object to a state significant data centre, and increased the number of public objections needed to trigger a referral from 50 to 100.

Advertisement

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has said new data centre projects must pay for their own energy, and must put at least as much energy back into the grid as they take out of it. The NSW inquiry found the rapid growth in electricity demand from data centres has the potential to hinder progress towards emission reduction targets if that growth isn’t matched by a similar growth in energy storage. Related Article Good Weekend AI data centres are springing up in communities across the country. Now, residents are fighting back Data centre proponents will have access to a 75-day express assessment process only if they comply with the state’s new data centre guidelines, which include funding additional water and energy supply. The report stopped short of calling for a pause on new data centre approvals after Labor and Liberal committee members voted together to remove the recommendation from the report. Lane Cove and Penrith councils used their evidence to call for a moratorium on new data centre approvals, citing concerns over community consultations and water and energy consumption. A NSW government spokesperson said many of the committee’s findings reflected what the government already heard while designing the state’s guidelines.
