The collapse of David Jones is expected to deliver a major blow to Brisbane’s retail centres across the city and further compound the sector’s struggles in the ailing Queen Street Mall. David Jones was handed over to administrators and receivers on Thursday, for the first time in its 188 years of trading, after its board voted to appoint voluntary administrators from McGrathNicol. The failed retailer’s lenders appointed FTI Consulting as receivers to the group, who will run the business until it is restructured and put up for sale. Brisbane’s CBD may be left without a department store if the David Jones store at QueensPlaza closes following the chain’s collapse into voluntary administration. Dominique Tassell The store was busier than usual on Thursday afternoon, both with people hoping to use their gift cards while they still could and with staff pulling down displays.

Advertisement

In the shoe section, brands including Steve Madden, Kurt Geiger and Dune had empty displays. A shopper told this masthead they had attempted to buy a pair of shoes but had been told by a staff member they were no longer able to be sold. Empty Steve Madden and Kurt Geiger shoe displays in the David Jones store at QueensPlaza in Brisbane’s CBD. Dominique Tassell Analysis by financial services firm MST Marquee identified all but two stores in Queensland as facing closure. There are four David Jones stores in Brisbane, located in Carindale, Chermside, the CBD and Indooroopilly. There are also two stores on the Gold Coast, at Pacific Fair and Robina, and one store in Sunshine Plaza on the Sunshine Coast.

Advertisement

MST Marquee expected all stores bar Chermside and Pacific Fair would close. However, QUT professor and retail expert Gary Mortimer said he believed the CBD store would remain open. An empty Dune shoe display in the David Jones store at QueensPlaza in Brisbane’s CBD. Dominique Tassell “There’s been no official announcement yet on which stores will close in Queensland,” he said. “QueensPlaza is a premium destination. That would be a store I would imagine would remain.” Mortimer said several stores that had undergone substantial redevelopment, such as Sunshine Plaza and Pacific Fair, would be less likely to close.

Advertisement

“I think there’s a future for this brand,” he said. “It is the oldest department store in the world, older than Harrods, older than Macy’s. There’s a lot of nostalgia and history connected to that brand, particularly here in Queensland.” The older shopping centres may be less attractive, Mortimer said. Previously, Myer stores have been replaced by retailers such as Kmart, Target and TK Maxx that are large but not big enough to fill the entire space. A closure of the David Jones in QueensPlaza would leave the CBD without a department store, after Myer vacated the old Myer Centre – now known as Uptown – in July 2023.

Advertisement

Vicinity Centres owns both QueensPlaza and Uptown, after it completed a takeover of the latter earlier this year. In its ASX announcement, Vicinity said it “maintains contingency plans for each of its David Jones locations and routinely assesses alternative uses for major tenancy space as part of its asset planning”. Experts argue there may be an excess of retail space in Brisbane’s CBD. Catherine Strohfeldt The company said in February the revitalised Uptown would combine fashion, dining, technology, leisure and entertainment stores, and would mirror the Emporium in Melbourne’s CBD. It estimated the redevelopment would cost $300-$350 million – funded through debt and the sale of other assets – and would be completed by 2029.

Advertisement

Advertisement

The proposal would replace the existing Wintergarden shopping centre with a six-storey retail podium topped by a 45-storey hotel, residential tower and a 16-storey office tower. Mortimer said there was an excess of retail space in the CBD, while locals have moved to centres such as Carindale and Chermside for their shopping. The old entrance to Myer from Queen Street Mall is still permanently closed, and the windows covered in hoarding. Marissa Calligeros “We don’t go into the CBD to shop any more, unless it’s for that luxurious experience which you get at QueensPlaza and Edward Street,” he said. “I think Wintergarden is well positioned to leverage that market, so I do think we will see a redeveloped Wintergarden. Potentially with a Myer store. Brisbane is the only capital city in Australia without a flagship Myer store.

Advertisement

“But of course that then creates some challenges for Uptown, which appears to have still not made any investment in that centre.” Rumours have swirled for years about a possible Myer comeback in the CBD, but none have eventuated, so exactly who would occupy all this retail space is up in the air. Empty shelves at the Indooroopilly David Jones. Mortimer said he would like to see Uptown, which has direct access to a bus station and plenty of parking, reinvigorated as a health services centre to accommodate workers and the growing number of people living centrally. David Jones’ collapse was triggered after the department store operator’s private equity owners failed to reach a deal with major landlord Scentre Group on store closures and its rent bill.

Scentre Group, which operates Westfield Carindale and Westfield Chermside, rejected a restructuring proposal put forward by David Jones. A counter-proposal by Scentre was subsequently rejected by David Jones’ board of directors on Wednesday. Related Article Analysis

Rusanow said its offer would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading. “That offer has disappointingly been rejected by them,” he said.

Children starting school will learn about financial concepts as part of maths lessons to keep the Australian curriculum relevant and help them grasp the foundational skills as international standings in numeracy slide. Education ministers announced the biggest change to the national curriculum in years on Thursday, including streamlining maths content in the first three years of school to ensure what students learn builds on itself. The main focus of foundation to year 2 remains on teaching maths, with the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority now breaking down content into explicit, sequential steps for teachers to follow. St Bernard’s School maths leader Nick Flavel with students Thea Nolan and Zavier Perez, who learn about cash in primary school despite growing up in an increasingly cashless society. Justin McManus But students will also encounter money in their lessons as a way of applying the concepts they learn and preparing them to have greater financial literacy in later years, with studies showing people confident in their numeracy skills often have higher financial and health outcomes.

Advertisement

“We’re not teaching five-year-olds about superannuation,” said ACARA chief executive Stephen Gniel. Related Article Opinion

Money psychology Why working harder won’t make you rich – and what to do instead Paridhi Jain Money contributor “We’re giving them the foundations they need to become financially literate adults. By developing essential mathematical skills such as addition, subtraction, multiplication and fractions, students build the knowledge and confidence they’ll need to understand more complex financial concepts later in life.” However, in an increasingly cashless society, teachers are grappling with how to introduce their youngest students to financial concepts. At St Bernard’s School in Coburg East, maths leader Nick Flavel said lessons still relied on teaching students about cash. “It’s a difficult concept to teach because we are living in a cashless and digital world. They have grown up watching their parents pay for things with a phone,” he said.

Advertisement

“They almost need something tangible there to understand it’s worth something. If it’s just a balance on a spreadsheet, then it almost doesn’t mean anything, but if there’s cash there, then it’s visibly worth something.” Related Article Education Maths enrolments rebound, but one group is taking longer to bounce back Carly Sawatzki, a senior lecturer at Deakin University who researches financial education in schools, said linking maths with financial literacy during early years helped bring real-world application to maths for many students, but only if they learnt about the world they were living in. “Many children don’t see financial exchange taking place with notes and coins,” Sawatzki said. “The challenge for the curriculum writers and then of course school teachers as well is to figure out well what other sorts of examples of financial exchange might be relevant for very young children to be learning about … Children might receive gift cards for cultural celebrations, for example, so that’s a different way they are experiencing money.”

Advertisement

Advertisement

The curriculum will now also ensure early primary school students learn about broad concepts of identity, family and belonging, before later learning about community, diversity and respect. Secondary school students will learn about antisemitism and other forms of hate in classes including history. These changes, which follow recommendations by David Gonski’s antisemitism education taskforce, accompany content about Jewish history, culture and its contributions to Australia more broadly at the request of the Jewish community, who did not want the new content to only focus on educating students about the Holocaust. Education ministers have also tasked the curriculum authority with investigating whether to make civics compulsory for year 9s and 10s nationwide after research showed high school students’ understanding of democracy had dropped to its lowest level since testing began in 2004. “Schools don’t just teach numeracy, literacy and critical thinking skills. The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.
